ACCOUNTING

          8244
        Paper 1



1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

The overall standard of the learners’ work has improved and there are fewer learners who were not able to cope with
the demands of Accounting AS level.

Teachers must emphasise the importance of dates (consisting of a day, month and year), names of contra accounts,
as well as layout of Statements among others.  It is also of vital importance that learners are taught to show their
calculations.

Learners have still misinterpreted some of the questions and did not answer what was asked.  Teachers are requested
to encourage learners to read the questions carefully and only answer what is asked.  Some learners could not apply
their knowledge to the questions asked.

Teachers need to teach learners that if a question asks the candidates to compare the difference must be shown and
they must not just state the facts.

The neatness of the learner ’s work needs improvement, especially with regards to numbers.  Learners must make their
digits clear and legible.  Abbreviations are not allowed.

1 (a) Fairly well answered.  Most of the learners defined fixed capital account correctly although they failed
           to give the reasons why a fixed capital account is preferred.  Some learners differentiated instead of
           giving reasons and some learners stated the features of partnerships.
           Answer:
           Fixed capital accounts
           -      When the partners' current accounts and capital accounts are kept separately.
           -      Therefore, the partners’ capital account balances will remain fixed to their initial capital contributions
                  each year. (1)

           Reasons why business may prefer fixed capital accounts
           -      If partners withdraw more than the profit share that they are entitled to, it is shown by a debit balance
                  on the current account (1)
           -      A debit balance acts as a warning (1)
           -      Fixed capital account makes it easier to calculate interest on capital (1)
           -      Partners are able to see amount invested.  Partners can differentiate between amount invested by
                  partners and amounts due to partners by the business or a debit balance which shows how much is
                  due by partners to a business (1) Any two [3]

(e)      Fairly well answered.  Although some learners knew what a debenture was, they failed to identify the
         features from the advantages.
         Answer:
         Features of debentures
         - Long-term loans evidenced by deeds which set out the rate of interest payable and the date of redemption
         - A debenture is a certificate that certifies that an amount is owed to someone
         - Instead of buying shares, some investors prefer to give these certified loans (debentures) to the company
           and to receive their money back after some time together with interest
         - It is considered the safest way to invest in a company since priority to repay the amount loaned is
           guaranteed by the certificate whether the business has made a profit or not
         - a company may issue shares as security to obtain debentures and redeem them later upon repayment
         - It is thus the easiest way to attract investment in the company and thus raise large sums of capital
         - it is treated as a liability since the company will have to repay the amount back with interest thereof
         - Interest on debenture is a financial expense to the company
         - if a company is wound up, debentures must be repaid before any capital is repaid to shareholders
         - Debenture holders are lenders:  they are not members of the company and are not entitled to vote at
           shareholders’ meetings
                                                                                                                                                                    Any three [3]

3.   POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

Teachers should coach learners to read carefully and with understanding, especially the requirements of a question and
to answer only what is asked.

Learners should show all workings and calculations as well as explain terminology in full sentences.

The correct definitions should be studied and not made up by students as they go along.

Learners must pay attention to dates, the correct account names and the correct layouts.

Learners should not only work on old examination papers, but as they tend to be threatened by questions with a different
format.

Teachers must plan enough time for revision and examination preparation.  They must pay attention to terminology.

The different level questions should be practised by teachers, especially the level C and D questions.

1.                     GENERAL COMMENTS


The paper of 2025 was of the same standard as the paper of 2024.  The difficulty level was the same as 2024, although
learners did not cope with the work in 2025, for various reasons.  Many questions, especially the theory questions were
misinterpreted  by  learners.    Learners  did  not  always  answer  what  was  asked.    Learners  were  supposed  to  first  give  a
specific answer and after that were supposed to elaborate on the “yes” or “no” answer, “should” or “should not” answer.

Managerial   accounting   counts   to   25%   of   the   total   marks   and   50%   of   the   marks   of   Paper   2.     This   topic   remains   a   big
problem for learners.  That is either because the topics were not dealt with in detail or were not taught at all.  This topic
is very important because of the weight it carries in the Paper 2.

3.    POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

Teachers are doing well in teaching a very full syllabus in 6 months.

A  suggestion  is  that  all  teachers  start  of  with  Managerial Accounting.   They  do  not  need  the  other  topics  to  be  able  to
do  Managerial Accounting.    It  counts  50%  of  Paper  2,  so  it  is  of  the  utmost  importance  that  this  topic  MUST  be  dealt
with  in  earnest.    Old  examination  papers,  also  old  Higher  papers  are  the  best  way  to  prepare  learners  for  Managerial
Accounting.

Teachers must teach learners to read the theory questions very well and break them up into parts if they want to do well
in theory questions.

The overall commitment from the teacher ’s side is there and by looking at the scripts, one can see that the syllabus has
been covered.

Teachers are recommended to stay positive and force the learners to do the theory questions by handing out old papers.
They  only  learn  how  to  answer  theory  if  they  practice  it.    Learners  tend  only  to  do  the Accounting  part  of  revision  and
write the theory questions down if the teacher provides the answers.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Most centres submitted the required documents and worksheets of good standard for external moderation.  A few
worksheets submitted were, however, not of acceptable standard.  Most centres submitted evidence in the form of
pictures as required.  Centres are encouraged to ensure that pictures submitted as evidence for practical investigations
are attached to specific investigation reports.  Pictures must be clear enough, well annotated and should show all major
stages of the investigation with candidates busy carrying out the tasks.  Centres that print their pictures in black and
white must ensure that the picture are clear otherwise colour pictures are more preferable than black and white pictures.
Candidates who are submitting typed reports are advised to use Arial / Times New Roman font and font size 12 with
1.5 line spacing.

Appropriateness of Assessment Tasks
Some centres selected all practical tasks from the same theme in the syllabus.  Thus, centres are advised to take
practical topics from different themes of the syllabus for fairness.  Some centres selected simple tasks that are not
challenging enough for candidates at this level.  Candidates should not only prepare seedbeds but should also grow
some vegetables on the prepared plots and take care of them till harvesting or marketing.  Similarly, for the task on seed
germination, which was selected by most centres, candidates should grow the viable seedlings and take care of them
until harvesting time.  Centres should take note that testing for soil pH alone is insufficient, thus, it should be extended
to regulation of the soil pH.  A food sample should be tested for at least two or more nutrients.  Centres can alternatively
test various samples for one nutrient.

Some centres selected topic tasks that were more of an investigation such as tropism.  Tasks should be hands-on,
allowing candidates to apply their technical skills by using tools and apparatus.  Some tasks did not assess any
practical skills as they were only addressing assessment objective B, such as cash flow statement, thus, they must be
discouraged in future.

Interpretation and application of assessment criteria
Most centres were aware of the five assessment criteria that should be assessed in each practical task and there was
a great improvement in the generation of marking points per marking criteria generated from various centres.  Few
centres submitted worksheets with theoretical questions.  Centres are urged to develop more challenging practical-
based questions by addressing Assessment Objective C, see page 17 of the syllabus, under the written component of
the worksheets.

Suitability and relevance of practical investigations
Selection of relevant question (hypothesis) for the investigation
Many candidates were able to come up with a hypothesis for their investigation.  However, some hypotheses were
not clearly formulated.  Examiners should provide appropriate guidance to help candidates in developing clear and
brief hypotheses.  Marks should then be awarded in accordance with the level of guidance provided by the examiner
as indicated in the marking criteria.  Some candidates selected topics that were not experimental such as surveys.
Selected topics should be of investigative nature, meaning candidates should find information for themselves by direct
observation and measurement.  See page 26 of Agricultural Science NSSCAS syllabus.

Planning of the investigation
It was evident that centres that did prior planning, produced investigations of an acceptable standard.  Candidates at
some centres opted for topics with more than one variable but failed to attend to all the variables such as influence of
organic fertilizer on germination, growth and yield as they only collected data on growth.  Some investigations required
a control such as the effect of manure on plant growth.  A control plot was required for comparative reasons to make
reasonable deductions.  Some candidates could not replicate their work.  Replication of treatments is necessary to
increase reliability.  Therefore, it is advisable for centres to guide candidates from the title selection until all the stages of
the investigations are exhausted.  However, teachers guiding the candidates should not do the work for candidates but
should  just  guide  and  allow  candidates  to  do  their  own  work.    Some  methodologies  were  shallow.  Methodology  is  the
backbone of the investigation and should include all aspects namely: methods used to plan, sample, measure, collect
and analyse data.

Handling of evidence
It was impressive to learn that most candidates showed understanding of how to handle data collected through completed
tables and graphs.  However, some candidates failed to label and scale their graphs correctly.  Results presented by
some candidates seemed unrealistic.  Candidates whose reports are handwritten are encouraged to use graph paper
for plotting graphs.  Thus, such centres should make graph paper available to candidates for such purposes.

Ability to make deductions
Most candidates could interpret and analyse their data.  However, interpretations were not supported by the data
collected.  Deductions conclusions made by some candidates were, however, not linked to the data collected or
hypotheses.  Examiners should ensure that candidates are guided to draw conclusions that are clearly linked to the
data collected and directly address the original hypothesis.  In addition, centres should ensure that candidates provide
clear and well-reasoned justifications for their conclusions.

Limitations
Most candidates were able to identify 1 or 2 limitations experienced during their investigations.  However, some
candidates   identified   challenges   that   what   already   been   addressed   during   the   investigation   and   therefore,   cannot   be
regarded as limitations.  Some recommendations suggested by candidates were not addressing the identified limitations.
Some identified limitations were not having suggestions on how they could be addressed or improved in future.  Centres
should guide and encourage candidates to suggest improvements that will help future researchers to overcome the
identified limitations.

Presentation, layout and originality
Many candidates were able to follow the report layout as outlined in the syllabus.  However, some candidates did not
indicate the brief plan of their practical investigations.  Candidates need proper guidance on how to write methodology.
Some candidates’ methodologies were not clearly describing what their investigations were all about.  Methodology
should give a clear insight into what the investigation entails.  Some candidates did not attach pictures or pictures
attached    were    insufficient.        Candidates    are    urged    to    attach    pictures    from    their    own    investigations    showing    all    major
steps and active participation of candidates.

Interpretation and application of assessment criteria for practical investigations
Most centres were able to interpret and apply the assessment criteria for practical investigation with regards to the six
marking criteria.  However, some centres did not adhere to the specific descriptors outlined within the marking criteria
such as maximum marks awarded for stating limitations even when no corresponding improvements were suggested.
Centres are urged to use the assessment criteria guide for practical investigations, when awarding marks for candidates’
practical investigations and to provide annotations as to how the marks were awarded.  Please see page 29 and 30 of
NSSCAS Syllabus for the criteria and guide to marking practical investigations.

Administration
It is appreciated that many centres complied with all the administrative procedures that are required for moderation
purposes and that some centres put in extra effort by providing the required information in neat and well-organised files.
This made the moderation exercise much easier.  Some errors in addition of marks were, however, detected.  Centres’
internal moderators should not only moderate and verify marks in the Assessment Summary form but are urged also to
ensure that marks are correctly transferred from the Candidate Individual Record Cards to the Continuous Assessment
Summary Form (CASF) and later to the MS1 form.

There was an improvement by most centres in submitting evidence of candidates’ work in the form of pictures, showing all
the main stages of the practical tasks and not just the end result.  It is important to verify before sealing the envelope that
all the necessary documents for external moderation are enclosed in the envelope.  Centres are referred to the reverse
side of the Individual Candidate Record Cards, Coursework Assessment Summary Forms for additional information.
In conclusion, the performance demonstrated by candidates was satisfactory.  We recommend that training be arranged
by      Regional      Offices      for      centres.          Agricultural      Science    Advanced      Subsidiary      level      teachers      should      seek      assistance
regarding the conducting and administering of School-Based Assessment in Agricultural Science.

1 B         This was very well answered. Most candidates correctly identified the hierarchical order

Introduction

We are living in a time where information can readily be found on the internet. This information, however, needs to be
understood and analysed                                                                                                                                                                     for accuracy as not all information found on the internet is always correct.  To be able to do
that, certain skills are taught at school and in Biology.

The following skills were tested in this examination paper:

•	                                Communication skills: The ability to read and understand a question and to express yourself in writing using
      whole sentences with correct punctuation and grammar.

•	                                              Numeracy skills: The ability to work with numbers given in standard notation, such as, 650 000 000 becomes
      6,5 x 108 and to interpret numerical information provided in a table.

•	                                              Problem-solving skills: The ability to apply learned content to new situations.

•	                                                          Work and study skills: The ability to answer a question by completing a diagram.  In Biology it is very helpful to make
      use of diagrams whilst studying.

•	                                       Critical and creative thinking skills: The ability to think logically, especially when describing processes.  Learners
      must learn to answer questions using their own knowledge, rather than repeating text from the textbook or the
      internet.

The text in italics is quoted from the Namibian National Curriculum Guidelines.  All these skills are needed to answer
a question paper successfully.  This requires factual knowledge, but also a good understanding of the content.  In
the 2025 examination, the recall questions were answered fairly well but questions requiring the application of that
knowledge were poorly answered by most candidates.

Key messages
Advanced Practical Skills is a laboratory-based practical paper focused on learners mastering the skills and competencies
relevant to the investigations outlined in the syllabus, rather than simply practising past examination questions. Learners
should be provided with sufficient time to engage in all practical activities within the syllabus, enabling them to develop
skills that are applicable both for the examination and for further studies or future employment.

General comments

It is advisable that AS learners                    demonstrate              an              advanced              level              of              proficiency              in              the              English                      language              to
comprehend scientific concepts thoroughly and accurately interpret questions, thereby enabling them to provide appropriate
responses.

Centres are urged to complete their reports meticulously and to observe the practical activities performed by the
learners, as the information contained in the Supervisor’s report is essential for the accurate assessment of
candidate’s answers during marking.

Candidates who have engaged with materials and apparatus during practical work as part of the course are generally
better prepared for the examinations. While the examination activities may not be entirely unfamiliar, candidates who
have    consistently    followed    instructions    in    a    variety    of    practical    tasks    typically    find    it    easier    to    organise    and    execute
original activities.

To ensure effective execution of a practical, candidates must carefully read the instructions, analyse the available data
required, and respond to questions based on the specific practical at hand, rather than rely on practical work completed
earlier in the academic year.

GENERAL COMMENTS
•	   Learners	demonstrated	a	solid	grasp	of	fundamental	chemistry	concepts	but	showed	inconsistency	in	applying	this
     knowledge	to	unfamiliar	situations.	While	most	performed	well	on	questions	requiring	straightforward	recall,	many
     struggled	with	higher-order	tasks,	such	as	justifying	the	choice	of	operating	temperature	in	the	Contact	process	and
     applying	the	mole	concept.
•	   There	   was	   clear	  evidence	     of	strong	   preparation	in	     fundamental	      areas	   such	   as	atomic	     structure	   and	  bonding.
     Learners	also	      demonstrated	solid	understanding	               of	 core	  topics	   basic	organic	     chemistry.	    Nonetheless,	notable
     gaps	appeared	in	physical	chemistry	(especially	mass	spectral	analysis)	and	in	introductory	inorganic	chemistry,
     including	explanations	of	periodic	trends	among	Period	3	elements..
•	   Learners	are	advised	to	pay	close	attention	to	the	command words	and	the	stem	of	each	question.	Underlining
     key	terms	can	help	in	identifying	exactly	what	the	question	requires.	For	instance,	in	Question	1,	learners	were
     asked	    to	state	the	ions	     responsible	for	each	peak,	yet	            some	provided	formulas	            of	 neutral	  atoms	or	    molecules
     despite	the	explicit	instruction	to	give	ions.	Additionally,	learners	should	read	questions	thoroughly	and	respond	only
     to	what	is	being	asked,	avoiding	unnecessary	detail.
•	   There	    was	  frequent	    misuse	    of	 technical	   terminology,	     particularly	   in	defining	    ionisation	   energy	    and	  describing
     variation	in	metallic	bonding	of	period	3	metals	and	maximum	oxidation	numbers	of	period	3	elements.	Learners
     should	be	encouraged	to	learn	precisely	certain	definitions,	trends	and	principles.	The	omission	of	a	single	key
     word	or	interchanging	some	words	can	lead	to	marks	not	being	awarded	if	it	is	an	important	part	of	the	definition.

     accurate	use	of	chemistry	terminology	is	welcomed	as	it	removes	ambiguity	from	responses.	Lengthier	responses
     or	the	inclusion	of	more	details	than	required	by	a	question	sometimes	led	to	contradictions	in	learners	answers.

                    MP2 prompt to enter sentence
                    MP3 correct loop (., ? or !) end mark to be catered for
                    MP4 split sentence into string words
                    MP5 count number of words and store in WordCount
                    MP6 check the last character in the sentence // determine sentence type
                    MP7 display WordCount, SentnceType
                    MP8 correct formatting e.g. indenting, meaningful variable names, or comments


                    Example Algorithm / Pseudocode
                    1. Initialise variables:
                       - sentence = ""    # Initialize an empty string to store the sentence
                       - WordCount = 0    # Initialize a variable to count words
                       - SentenceType = "" # Initialize a variable to store the type of sentence
                    2. Display a prompt for the user to enter a sentence.
                    INPUT sentence
                    3. Loop until an end mark (., ?, or !) is encountered:
                       a. Read a character from the user.
                       b. Append the character to the 'sentence' string.
                    4. Split the 'sentence' string into words using spaces as delimiters:
                       a. Initialize a list 'words' to store the words.
                      b. Initialize an empty string 'CurrentWord' to build each word.
                       c. Loop through each character in 'sentence':
                          i. If the character is a space:
                             - Add 'CurrentWord' to the 'words' list (if 'CurrentWord' is not empty).
                             - Reset 'CurrentWord' to an empty string.
                          ii. Otherwise, append the character to 'CurrentWord'.
                    5. Add the last 'CurrentWord' to the 'words' list (if not empty).
                    6. Count the number of words in the 'words' list and store it in 'wordCount'.
                    7. Check the last character in the 'sentence' string to determine the sentence type:
                       a. If the last character is '.', set 'SentenceType' to "statement."
                       b. If the last character is '?', set 'SentenceType' to "question."
                       c. If the last character is '!', set 'SentenceType' to "exclamation."
                    8. Display the following information:
                       - The number of words in the sentence (WordCount).
                       - The type of sentence entered (SentenceType).
                    9. End the program.

                    sentence = ""
                    WordCount = 0
                    SentenceType = ""

        break

# Split the sentence into words

# Count the number of words

# Determine the sentence type

elif sentence.endswith('!'):
    SentenceType = "exclamation"


# Display the information

print(f"Sentence type: {SentenceType}")

9(f)(ii)                                                          In electronics, a Schmitt trigger is a comparator circuit with hysteresis 3                                                                                                              AOVR:
              implemented by applying positive feedback to the noninverting input of a                                                             1 x 3
              comparator or differential amplifier.  It is an active circuit which converts an
              analogue input signal to a digital output signal.  The circuit is named a trigger
              because the output retains its value until the input changes sufficiently to
              trigger a change. In the non-inverting configuration, when the input is higher
              than a chosen threshold, the output is high. When the input is below a different
              (lower) chosen threshold the output is low, and when the input is between
              the two levels the output retains its value.  This dual threshold action is called
              hysteresis and implies that the Schmitt trigger possesses memory and can
              act as a bi-stable multi-vibrator (latch or flip-flop).  There is a close relation
              between the two kinds of circuits: a Schmitt trigger can be converted into a
              latch and a latch can be converted into a Schmitt trigger.
              Schmitt trigger devices are typically used in signal conditioning applications
              to remove noise from signals used in digital circuits, particularly mechanical
              contact bounce in switches.  They are also used in closed loop negative
              feedback configurations to implement relaxation oscillators, used in function
              generators and switching power supplies.

From   the   responses   of   the   candidates   on   the   questions,   there   were   no   problems   answering   the   questions.   However,
good responses were given for certain questions and candidates could score good marks.
Evidence   also   shows   that   quite   a   few   candidates   did   not   have   the   knowledge   and   skills   to   answer   certain   questions
successfully. This situation can only be mastered when more training is given to teachers on how to teach the syllabus
successfully. It can illuminate this situation. By the spread of marks for this question paper, it looks acceptable, but there
are a few of areas which need to improve.

COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

      (a) Analysis
            Candidate should not write a fictional story about the reason why the product should be made.  The situation
            and information given in the paper may not simply be copied or repeated from the paper as an answer.
            Candidates   should   analyse   the   given   problem.      That   means   to study                                                                                                           (something) closely and carefully,
            to find the nature of the given problem by a close and careful examination. How can the problem be solved.
            Appropriate factors should be considered.  Candidates should think of, and record all the additional information,
            like: tools, construction, materials.

      (b)   Specifications
            Candidates may not copy the specifications given  in the paper.
            Candidates can generate other specifications taking into consideration of the following guideline:
            Functionality, ergonomics, aesthetics, materials and construction.
            Generic      responses      must      be      avoided.            These      specifications      must      be      relatively      specific.      Some      candidates
            stated     generic specifications like “it must be safe, must look nice, etc.” Specifications must also be justified
            with reasoning.
            A   specification   could   look   as   follows:   E.g.   “The   product   must   be   made   out   of   aluminium,   because   it   is   light
            weight and does not corrode.”

      (c)   Design solutions
            Many ideas were not in line with the criteria given.  Candidates should draw the ideas according to the
            specifications given.  Candidates should come up with a minimum of four possible solutions for them to be
            marked under high band.  Most candidates came up with three possible solutions which made candidates to
            lose marks.
            Ideas should also be drawn three dimensionally.
            Detail should be shown in the sketches, many notes should be written.
            Measurements should be added. More than three ideas should be drawn.
            Ideas should be adequately rendered / coloured and enhanced.
            The ideas should also be evaluated.
            Communication has its own marks awarded from 0 – 4marks. Candidates should work hard on their
            sketches to get all the marks.

(d)     Development of proposed solution
               This is the part where candidates of some centres lost valuable marks. In this section of the question paper
               the candidates should take the chosen idea and make further detailed decisions on form, materials and
               construction methods to be used in the final product. In some cases, candidates did not do a sufficient
               development of the final idea.
               This is not simply a repetition of one of the ideas recorded in the previous section.
               The candidates should show processes that are to be followed in the manufacturing and also show                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          details
               of construction.
               Rendering / colouring should be done and measurements should be added.
               The development should also be evaluated.
               Communication showing the expected                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   solution has its own marks awarded from 0 – 4marks. Candidates
               should work hard on their development sketches to get all the marks.

GENERAL COMMENTS

Centres must be commended for the completion and submission of coursework samples from all regions.  The quality of
coursework for NSSCAS 2025 was generally of a better standard. There were some centres that produced coursework
that is below average. This indicates that the candidates were not correctly guided by the teacher, or that the candidates
were reluctant to follow the guidance of the teacher. Regional Offices should make sure that Centre Reports are studied
and recommendations drafted for implementation purposes are forwarded from the regions to the schools.

Regional Office should target schools that did not perform well and investigate what the reason is for the substandard
results. In the cases where teachers are not sure what is expected in the folders, they should be trained to ensure that
the candidates can be taught how to compile a folder correctly. On the other hand, if the teacher is not performing, the
principal and head of department at the school should be informed to continuously monitor the work done by the teacher
and the progress of the candidates on the project folders. If possible networking with DNEA, NIED and other regions
with   Senior   Education   Officers   as   well   as   relevant   stakeholders   should   be   initiated   to   have   teachers   capacitated   and
assisted on a regular basis. It appears at some centres, the common mistakes made during 2024, were repeated in
the 2025 design folders. This indicates that the learners were not taught correctly by the teacher. A conclusion could be
drawn that Centre Reports are not studied and recommendations not implemented by these centres. Due to the defiant
negligence by some centres, the assistance of the Regional Directors is needed to make sure that Senior Education
Officers and Circuit Inspectors study and analyse these reports and monitor that the recommendations are implemented
at schools that present Design and Technology as a subject.

It is commendable that some centres have read and adhered to the advice given is the respective centre reports. Once
again, Regional Offices, principals and HOD’s are pleaded to take the responsibility of ensuring that folders and projects
are monitored throughout the year in future, especially at the centres where the candidates performed poorly. Towards
the end of the second term the folders should be internally moderated before the marks are dispatched to DNEA for
external moderation. Regional Offices must make sure that NSSCAS schools are provided with the necessary materials,
tools  and  safety  equipment  for  candidates  to  build  quality  products.  DNEA  observed  that  some  centres’  projects  were
compromised by the lack of adequate resources. It is shocking to observe in the photographic evidence included in
the folders, that candidates saw wooden boards on a circular saw not using a fence. Photographs show candidates
sawing wood with their fingers dangerously close to saw blad pushing wood when the blade is running. If a candidate
is to be injured, or loses a finger, under these circumstances, the teacher responsible, as well as the ministry could be
held accountable. A teacher may never let candidates work in the workshop without proper supervision. Candidates
who are not submitting sufficient photographic evidence is a problem when the projects are be moderated. The sample
of work presented for moderation was suitable in most cases and centres generally applied the assessment criteria
appropriately, although, in some cases, this was not at the correct level.

All folders must include clear photographic evidence of the artefacts, in addition to an overall view of the final product,
showing detail to support the awarding of marks.

If sufficient photographic evidence is not submitted, the candidates’ marks will be affected negatively.

COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC ASSESSMENT HEADINGS

Defining
Some of the candidates clearly stated the problem to be addressed but not all gave a concise Design Brief. Candidates
should be encouraged to complete adequate and relevant research in order to form a suitable knowledge base after
formulating   the   Brief.      Only   then   can   the   specifications   be   listed.  These   specifications   must   be   relatively   specific   and
must be justified. Some candidates stated generic specifications like “it must be safe” or “must not be big or too small”,
etc. Some candidates included points of specification, but of a generic nature which could be applied to any product.

Research

Some centres research consisted of irrelevant information that was simply written in a paragraph form. This did not lead
the candidate to an idea of what the outcome of the product should be.

Candidates should do research into similar existing products as mentioned in the Design Brief and evaluate these
products regarding cost, material, suitability etc.

Then additional information regarding the processes, material and fittings should be researched to see what is available
locally.

Conceptualising

This is where candidates can show evidence of genuine design creativity. Imaginative and innovative handling of a good
range of concepts and ideas is of essence. Most candidates included a wide range of different ideas enhanced by clearly
annotated sketches. In some cases candidates presented a few drawings that showed too little design capabilities and
tended to follow a single concept. These ideas can be presented most successfully through neatly rendered sketches
and candidates should be encouraged to include notes and dimensions. Annotations should include comments on the
construction, joining methods and materials. Then it is important that the each idea is evaluated as to how an idea might
link  to  the  specification.    Placing  photocopies  of  drawings  in  a  folder  is  not  acceptable,  because  they  could  be  copied
from someone else’s work.

Development

In      most      cases      candidates’      developments      met      the      expected      criteria,      but      in      a      few      cases      this      part      was      neglected      or
inadequate.

In this section of the folder the candidates should take only the chosen idea and make further detailed decisions on
form,   materials   and   construction   methods   to   be   used   in   the   final   product.   Ideas   should   be   fully   developed   with   good
attention to detail. Candidates are expected to show deep insight and good command of related knowledge. In some
cases    candidates    found    it    difficult    to    apply,    and    in    these    cases    the    final    ideas    were    simply    a    repetition    of    one    of    the
ideas recorded in the previous section. Candidates are expected to also illustrate every step of production with notes
describing the action.

In  most  cases  the  final  drawings  of  the  Design  Solution  were  generally  well-presented  and  gave  sufficient  information
with regards to the manufacturing of the product.

Presentation

Candidates  were  expected  to  show  refined  graphical  skills  including  fluent  freehand  and  precise  measured  drawings.
Most centres could produce drawings with good command of rendering and other enhancement which is commendable.
Centres in the top band produced excellent communication skills and had their work well managed and attractively laid
out.

The following is expected: An isometric drawing / sketch with dimensions and notes. (rendered), an exploded view
(rendered) an orthographic drawing showing detailed dimensions. Then also a cutting list, other material list, a table
showing time planning and a flowchart showing the sequential steps of production.

Product realization (Control; Technical; Product)

Photographic evidence showed that some candidates were able to work on their own and able to work at an acceptable
standard   of   construction   and   finish   to   the   extent   that   the   end   product   could   be   used.   Sadly,   some   centres   could   not
provide      sufficient      photographic      evidence      to      substantiate      the      credibility      of      the      folders.      Some      photographic      evidence
is  just  a  mere  posing  activity  and  no  real  action  is  seen  which  made  it  difficult  for  the  moderator  to  clearly  distinguish
various safe approaches and processes from the photos.

Notably, photographic evidence showed some candidates operating power tools (such as angle grinders) without the
required protective clothing (leather gloves, eye protection), an unsafe practise that should be prohibited. The teacher
may not allow the candidates to work in

Clear photos of the candidate doing all the processes, as well as clear photos showing the final product. The candidate
must be seen working in the pictures.

Testing and Evaluation

Some candidates included photographic evidence to show the testing of the product, which is commendable. They are,
however, encouraged to link the outcome of the original specifications and make objective judgements on the success
of their products. The section should also include suggestions for further modifications or possible future improvements.
Therefore,   centres   are   implored   to   ensure   that   specifications   are   fully   evaluated   and   tested   in   this   section,   which   will
guarantee maximum marks for the candidates.

Conclusion

Even though the coursework received from the centres for NSSCAS was at a high standard in most cases, it is clear that
centres offering NSSCAS Design and Technology for 2025 as a subject, and failed to achieve good marks, need to get
a d training to standardize the general understanding on the different sub-topics for the design folders.

GENERAL COMMENTS

There was an improvement in the quality of candidates’ work this year, although there are still some concerns:
•	                                           The lack of punctuation is becoming an issue.
•	                                           In some places, punctuation is used incorrectly, leading to poor sentence structure.
•	                                           Contractions, slang and over-generalisation should be addressed.
•	                                           The use of a lowercase “i” when referring to oneself is widespread.
•	                                           Errors of subject-verb agreement are also becoming increasingly prominent.
•	                    The	repetition	of	the	infinitive	“to	go	work”,	“to	go	look”	had	occurred	in	many	scripts.
•	                                           The use of idioms and proverbs should be applied carefully.
•	                                           Too many essays are still exceeding the word count.
•	                                            Sloppy handwriting hampers understanding and reading, which could result in a poor mark.
•	                               Candidates are frequently starting sentences with dangling or unrelated participle, such as  “Running  down the
     road, I saw..”, which makes grammar weaker.
The	use	of	the	       prefix	“in”	  joined	with	the	use	        of	 “in”	 as	 a	preposition	     is	 common	among	candidates,	                for	example:
“inlove” “infront” “inconclusion”, etc.  Some teachers seem to ignore this clumsy error.  Similarly, words such as “aswell”,
“eachother”,” eventhough”, are not being picked up.
Candidates seem not to know the difference between “were” and “where”, “its” and “it’s”, “their” and “there” “advise”
and”advice”, “practise” and “practice”.  These issues should be addressed.  Slang such as “gonna” and “wanna” is
unacceptable in standard English.  Common words are spelled incorrectly.  Negligence seems to play a role here.
Sentences should not begin with “so”.  Words such as “like” and “nice” should be avoided.
Essays	are	sometimes	based	on	themes	rather	than	on	the	specific	topics.	 	Learners	need	to	be	taught	to	answer
the	question	and	not	write	broadly	on	the	theme	or	field.	 	Failure	to	adhere	to	this	will	result	in	a	poor	mark,	if	any.
Sometimes,	large	parts	of	the	plot	are	crossed	out	which	makes	reading	and	understanding	difficult.
Many	candidates	deliberately	wrote	in	very	small	handwriting	in	order	to	fit	in	a	plot	that	far	exceeded	the	word	count.
This practice should be addressed by teachers, as it if unfair to candidates who adhere to the word limit.  In many cases,
this approach is futile, as candidates penalise themselves through repetitive ideas, resulting in a weak plot in anyway.


COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1:  Citizenship

It should be mandatory for all citizens aged eighteen and above to vote in local and national elections.  Outline and
explain your views.

This was the compulsory question and was attempted with mixed results.  The meaning of “mandatory” appeared to
be problematic, as many candidates misinterpreted the question.  The question required a discussion or argument
about	whether	voting	should	            be	mandatory.	  	Many	candidates	wrote	broadly	                    about	the	     field	of	“Citizenship”	      rather
than	addressing	the	specific	topic	or	the	concept	of	voting	as	a	right	or	responsibility.		The	more	successful	candidates
understood that the focus was on voters being “forced” to vote, which was the issue they needed to discuss.  It was not
enough for candidates simply to repeat the topic.  In some cases, the development of ideas did not clearly show the
candidates’ viewpoints, resulting in confusion regarding the application of the concept of mandatory or forced voting.

Question 2:  Social trends

The	influence	of	the	media	on	teenagers	can	deprive	them	of	having	heathy	relationships	and	developing	social	skills.
How far do you agree?

This	was	a	very	popular	choice,	with	mixed	results.	 	Candidates	should	have	argued	the	influence	of	the	media	on
relationships and social skills, rather than generalising about social media itself.  Many candidates discussed social
trends instead of the effect of media on teenagers.  The disadvantages and disadvantages of social media were covered
in many essays.  Most essays focused on social media rather than media in general.  Many candidates had litttle
understanding of what social skills are.  Some candidates, however, were able to produce strong essays that discussed
the effects of media on the development of social skills and on building healthy relationships.

Question 3: The Arts

“My shocking revelation about a world-famous piece of art shattered relationships between nations, and I became a
wanted person.”  Tell your story.

A few candidates attempted this topic, which was also the most misinterpreted.  Candidates were expected to discuss
how the revelation of a famous art piece caused worldwide turmoil and led to the artist becoming a wanted person.
Instead, many plots told a success story.  General knowledge of the arts was severely lacking; as a result, the Mona
Lisa	was	the	only	painting	most	candidates	could	think	of.		Some	plots	focused	on	the	theft	or	destruction	of	an	art	piece.
This approach led to weak results.

Question 4: Travel and Transport

The economic progress of a country is determined by the quality of its infrastructure.  What are your views?

This topic was attempted by a few candidates, with mixed results.  Candidates should have elaborated on how good
infrastructure leads to income and, as a result, economical progress.  They needed to link quality infrastructure to
economic development.  Many candidates confused the concept of “economic progress” and “quality infrastructure”.
Many had little understanding of what “quality infrastucture” entails.   Some plots focused on tourism, travel and transport
in general, which resulted in poor marks.

Question 5: Language and communication

His powerful words convinced me that I had not failed but that I had gained valuable experience. Relate the event that
led to this realisation.

This was the most successful topic.  Candidates were expected to relate a story in which they attempted something,
failed and were encouraged by someone’s powerful words to achieve success.  Many did not link the two main ideas.
Some even produced lengthy motivational speeches or simply discussed language as a tool.  A few plots were also
mundane.

Positive suggestions to teachers

Language	lessons	are	crucial.		Concord,	tenses	and	style	must	be	taught	and	practised.		Greater	general	knowledge
is also needed.

Emphasis on reading, comprehension and interpretation skills is vitally important.  Extensive reading expose learners
to sophisticated and correct use of language, which they can absorb and incorporate into their own writing.  Reading is
key.		Learners	should	be	encouraged	to	summarise	the	articles	they	have	read.

Spelling	is	a	major	concern.	 	Extensive	reading	will	help	address	this.	 	Learners	should	avoid	or	practise	not	using
colloquialisms such as kids, guys.   They should also avoid tailor-made responses; it is evident that some learners write
essays	beforehand	and	then	try	to	force	them	into	a	particular	field	or	theme.		Word	limits	must	be	strictly	adhered	to.

Learners	must	number	their	topics.		Many	fail	to	do	so,	leaving	the	examiner	to	figure	out	which	topic	was	developed.

Expressions such as “very crucial”, “very essential” should be avoided.

Use the correct pronoun.  DO NOT WRITE, for example, “They still vote for whoever you want”.

Learners	lack	general	knowledge,	and	mundane	discussions	or	plots	result	in	poor	marks.		Accurate	sentence	structures
must be practised, and paragraphing should also be emphasised.  The appropriate use of tenses needs to be taught.

 Model answer: Rossing Uranium Mine

 The utilisation of natural resources in Namibia is governed by several Acts, notably the Minerals (Prospecting
 and Mining) Act 33 of 1992, the Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013, and the Forest Act 12 of 2001.
 Rössing Uranium Mine, a mine in Namibia is adhering to these Acts which regulate its mining rights, water use
 and environmental protection. Rössing adheres to these laws through licensing, water management schemes
 and biodiversity conservation initiatives.
 The Minerals (Prospecting and Mining) Act 33 of 1992:  The Minerals Act governs the exploration and exploitation
 of Namibia’s mineral resources. It requires enterprises to obtain mining licenses, conduct Environmental Impact
 Assessments (EIAs), and submit Environmental Management Plans (EMPs).
 Rössing   Uranium   Mine   operates   under   mining   licenses   issued   by   the   Ministry   of   Mines   and   Energy.  The   mine
 prepares EMPs and EIAs before expansions or new projects. It reports production, safety and compliance
 measures to authorities, ensuring transparency and accountability. Through these measures, Rössing
 demonstrates adherence to the Minerals Act by balancing economic extraction with environmental safeguards.
 Water is a scarce resource in Namibia, making its management critical. The Water Resources Management
 Act      11      of      2013      regulates      its      use,      and      conservation      of      water      resources,      requiring      permits      thereby      promoting
 sustainable practices. Rössing Uranium Mine relies on NamWater ’s supply scheme, which is regulated under the
 Act. The mine implements water recycling and treatment systems to minimise wastage. Continuous monitoring
 ensures that water discharged meets legal quality standards. By adopting efficient water management practices,
 Rössing aligns with the Act’s objectives of sustainability and pollution control.
 Although Namibia is largely arid, forest and vegetation resources remain vital for biodiversity and environmental
 health. The Forest Act 12 of 2001provides for conservation, fire prevention, and sustainable use of forest produce.
 Rössing Uranium Mine undertakes biodiversity monitoring and vegetation management programs. Rehabilitation
 projects include replanting indigenous species in disturbed areas. Fire prevention measures are enforced to
 comply        with        forest        fire        control        provisions.        These        initiatives        reflect        Rössing’s        commitment        to        environmental
 stewardship under the Forest Act.
 Obtaining mining licenses, water permits and environmental approvals under the Acts is costly since it includes
 legal fees, environmental studies and ongoing audits. The Acts impose limits on water usage, land use and
 vegetation clearance. These restrictions can slow down expansion projects and reduce operational flexibility.
 The Forest Act and Minerals Act require rehabilitation of mined land and biodiversity monitoring. This adds long-
 term costs for replanting, soil stabilisation and environmental reporting.
 However, these Acts ensure resources are not depleted which secures the mine’s long-term viability and
 operational continuity. Compliance with legislation builds trust with government, communities, and international
 stakeholders.  It  enhances  the  mine’s  reputation  and  reduces  conflict. Adhering  to  the Acts  minimises  pollution,
 land degradation and ecological damage. This reduces liability risks and potential penalties, while aligning with
 global sustainability standards.
 While  the Acts  impose  financial  and  operational  costs,  they  also  come  with  benefits  by  ensuring  sustainability,
 protecting    the    environment    and    strengthening    stakeholder    relations.    For    Rössing    Uranium    Mine,    the    balance
 leans toward long-term gains, as compliance secures both continued access to resources and international
 credibility in the uranium market.
 It        is,        therefore,         evident         that        the       Acts        that        govern         the         utilisation         of        natural         resources         are         beneficial         to        the
 entrepreneurs.     When     Rossing     Uranium     complies     with     the   Acts,     it     leads     to     building     a     good     reputation     for     the
 enterprise, which can attract investors who may provide extra funds to expand the mine and, therefore, the
 enterprise     will     be     sustained     in     the     long     run.          Since     Rossing     Uranium     is     a     profit-driven     enterprise,     it     may     not
 fully comply with the Acts, as the government controls the volume of minerals to be extracted which leads to
 lower      productivity      and,      therefore,      Rossing      mine      might      experience      low      sales      which      will      result      in      lower      profit.
 Consequently, non-compliance may lead to penalties, suspension or a permit revoked.

            à-vis, successful responses did well with clear stipulations and parameters, going further to give a
            post-mortem of the event in a bid to display long-lasting impact.  Responses were expected to be
            formal.  Some had colloquial vocabulary like ‘vibe’; ‘chill’ ‘, crazy’ amongst others. Spelling errors were
            visible in these, exited for excited, principle for principal, excreta for etcetera, high schoolers for high
            schooler or pupils or learners, to mention a few.  Stronger responses successfully responded to the
            question.  Most candidates were familiar with the conventions of a news story.  More so, the concerts
            had names and venues. Paragraphs were expected to be shorter with simple to complex sentences in
            use.  Of note, some of the best responses displayed new or uncommon vocabulary in the responses,

1 (b) Even    though    there    was    a    general    improvement    in    responding    to    the    reflective    commentary,    many
            candidates still struggled to write reflectively.   Hence, the reflective style needs more attention: most
            learners       tend       to       merely       analyse       their       writing       without       reflecting       on       it.       Generally,       most       candidates
            managed to discuss form, structure and language with varying success.   While others managed,
            some fell short by discussing one out of three or both language and structure and leaving out the
            others. This led to poor responses as some candidates narrated without the correct structure, which is
            Point, Evidence, Example (PEE). All points on Form, Language and Structure must be fully discussed
            in a balanced manner, using clear examples.  Merely stating that discourse markers were used is not
            a reflection whatsoever and cannot be awarded marks.  The same goes for just mentioning the uses
            of linguistic devices and short sentences without displaying the effect thereof regarding the creation
            of the atmosphere and the impact of the concert.  In addition, often the discussions became generic
            instead of text-specific. Simply stating that discourse markers were used to create a flow in writing can
            still only warrant a ‘limited’ mark band.

General
The general standard of this session was satisfactory.
Some candidates appeared to struggle with time management, leading to the second question was either rushed or
incomplete. All but a few candidates managed to demonstrate at least a basic understanding of their selected texts, and
many showed signs of genuine engagement with them.
Poetry and All the Bright Places      remained      the      most      popular      genres      this      year.    Answers      reflecting      a      wide      range      of
performances were seen on each of the texts attempted by the candidates.
Candidates should use their introductions (thesis statements) to set out generally their interpretation of both the text and
the question as a framework on which their analysis can be structured.
Furthermore,    rhetorical questions should be avoided as a literary essay focuses on analysis of the given text.
Candidates should focus on the ways the writers use language, form and style to create meaning. If a learner continuously
uses “then” it reflects a narrative summary or paraphrase of the given text.
Moreover, the focus should not be confused with writing an analytical essay based on style, structure and language.
The focus in a literary essay is always on the way writers present the text, not on who the target audience is or the main
purpose of the text.
While language is not assessed in this paper, many candidates demonstrated weakness in spelling, expression and
sentence structure which may impede meaning.
Candidates should avoid writing in the first or second person as well as starting their sentences with “the poem talks
about...” Many candidates also use ‘author,’ ‘poet’ and ‘playwright’ interchangeably.
General Mark Scheme:
Use    the    generic    mark    scheme    levels    to    find    the    mark.    Place    the    answer    in    a    level    first.    Look    for    the    “best    fit”    of    the
answer into a level. An answer needs to show evidence of most, but not necessarily ALL, of the qualities described in a
level in order to be placed in that level. Then award a mark for the relative position of the answer within the level.
Candidates may address the question in many different ways. There is no one required answer or approach.  Also avoid
penalising answers for leaving out a particular focus. Reward what is there, showing what you are rewarding in your
comments.
Consider all strands and weigh up the performance as a whole in placing the answer in a level, then show that you have
done so in the summative comment.
Each answer is marked out of 25, in accordance with the general marking criteria.
Assessment objectives
All assessment objectives are equally weighted, and all are considered in assessing each essay.
Each level in the marking criteria is divided into strands corresponding to the assessment objectives:
L1: Knowledge and understanding                                        (K/U)
L2: Analysis                                          (AN)
L3: Personal response                                        (P)
L4: Communication                                        (C)

Positive suggestions to teachers:
•    Teachers should discourage candidates from using superfluous expressions such as “brilliant author”, “insightful
     use of imagery” or “the author ’s exceptional use of lexis”. These expressions are arbitrary and do not constitute a
     personal response.
•    Whenever a reference is made to literary techniques such as the structure of the poem, rhyme and rhythm, imagery
     or pathos or ethos, it is imperative that candidates give a reason why it is important and link it to the requirements
     of the question. They have to focus on very specific effects created.
•    Teachers should instruct candidates not to start their answers with a quote. It is better to teach candidates to start
     their writing with a solid thesis statement, which they then continue to prove by using strong points, evidence and
     analysis.
•    Also note that when analysing an extract or poem, it is imperative to focus on the entire text. If a poem has seven
     stanzas, the importance of all the stanzas in relation to the task needs to be discussed. Moreover, when answering

the (b) part of the question paper, candidates should not rely heavily on parts outside the given extract.
•      Line references do not suffice. Candidates must quote and explain the effectiveness of the quote in relation to their
       thesis statement or topic sentence.
•      It is not necessary at this level to explain literary devices. Rather than discuss the effect created  by  the  specific
       image, we would rather waste time providing a definition.
•      Responses which rely on a summary of the set texts are not successful.
•      Successful responses focus closely on the writing of the texts and how the writer presents the meaning and content
       to the reader.
•      Successful       responses       use       analysis       of       specific       references       and       quotations       to       support       the       points       made.      This       is
       particularly important for the (a) questions, where candidates select their own references to answer the question
•      There is no word count                                                                                                                                   requirement for this paper. Please discourage candidates from spending time on counting
       words.
•      Candidates should avoid vague phrases such as “and so much more” or “of sorts”. They should also not use
       general adjectives such as “good” and “bad” as these are      vague descriptors and do not constitute a thorough
       analysis.
•      Encourage candidates not to use “author” “poet” and “playwright” interchangeably. Candidates should also use
       “novel” instead of “the book”.
•      Encourage candidates to use PEEL paragraphs. Each paragraph should have a clear                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                topic sentence,                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          explanation
       and evidence which link to the requirements of the question and their thesis statement in their introduction.
•      Language is not assessed in this component, but common spelling errors or using advanced vocabulary incorrectly
       can impede meaning. Encourage candidates to use simple (but complete) sentences and emphasise that correct
       (British) spelling is still important. Candidates should not use advanced vocabulary if they do not know the meaning.

COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1


(a)   This   question   asked   candidates   to   comment   on   how   the   author   uses   language   and   style   to   convey   his
      strong feelings and opinions about the concept of Ubuntu.
      This question proved to be understood by the candidates whereby they could link the feelings and opinions
      of the author to the language and style used by the author.  It was good to see that most of the candidates
      could identify different phrases in the passage, explain them and describe their uses in the passage.
      At  some  centres  candidates  identified  punctuation  marks  as  symbols,  describing  insignificant  phrases  and
      could not be credited for that.
      •     No identification of punctuation marks and its use is needed.
      •     Answers on language and style differ from texts (passages) to texts (passages).  It means different features
            of language and style will be identified which could not be found in other texts used and not the same parts
            of speech.

(b)   Candidates      were      asked      to      write      a      speech      as      a      primary      school      teacher      who      had      heard     Thabo      Mbeki
      delivering the speech.  The children in the school asked what the president said.  Using mostly your own
      words, write what you plan to say to them.  Base your answer on the material in the original speech.
      This question was well-attempted by a number of candidates.
      •     Some candidates did not understand but followed the instructions well.  They could not plan and identify
            the  main  parts  (information)  of  the  speech  which  was  supposed  to  be  simplified  into  Khoekhoegowab
            according   to  the  language   level  (ability)  of  primary  school  learners  and  how  these  learners  can  make
            use of the Ubuntu concept in their daily lives.
      •     Some  of  the  candidates  still  do  not  know  the  structures  of  speech,  and  or  how  to  write  them  as  some
            started with the introductory paragraph:  greetings and identifying of different audiences present, which
            others did not do that.

Centres are advised to attend to the following:
•     Work  more  on  language  and  style  on  different  texts, meaning, identification  in  a  passage  and  how  to apply  it into
      (a) questions.
•     Stick to the word limit (120 – 150 words).  Only the main part was needed!
•     Attend to the context, audience and purpose. It is the appropriate language used that determines whether the text
      is well-written and not the so-called “format” of the text.
•     Candidates should be given exercises on how to re-use any language from the original passage.
•     Pay more attention to written work, such as letters, speeches or summary writing.
•     Candidates    should    be    prepared    to    give    a    holistic    commentary    instead    of    bits    and    pieces    (isolated    fragments    of
      meanings of phrases and individual words with no effect on the question).

1      GENERAL COMMENTS

       Strengths
       •	                                            Creativity and engagement:  Many learners attempted original ideas, unusual images and personal touches
             to their writing which portrayed a level of creativity and originality.
       •	                                           Understanding of topic and prompts:  Most of the candidates could understand and answer the question
             paper to the best of their abilities, although some of them had limited vocabulary and could not express
             themselves well.
       •	                                           Use of anecdote:  For narrative tasks, several learners used a personal story effectively to ground their
             piece and create means for their writing to flow as required by the topics.
       •	                                           Recognition of audience:  In some discursive pieces, learners adjusted tone and register, especially with
             the voice overs; their tone became more conversational and joyful as required by the topic.
       •	                                     Attempted structure:  Many answer scripts showed an awareness of structural features (introduction/body/
             conclusion).
       •	                                           Neat and eligible writing:  Many learners wrote neatly and eligibly.

       Weaknesses
       •	                                 Lack of clear introductions and conclusions:  Many learners failed to establish context or wrap up their
             ideas effectively.
       •	                                        Elongated approaches to the answering the questions:  Some of the candidates answered the questions
             with unrelated narration and only attempted to answer the question in the last paragraphs.
       •	                                               Poor paragraphing and number of words:  Ideas were often jumbled together without logical progression or
             thematic grouping while not sticking to the number of words.
       •	                                           Inconsistent tenses:  Learners frequently shifted between past and present tense, disrupting narrative flow                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        .
       •	                                                    Limited vocabulary:  Overuse and change of basic idioms and figures of speech (e.g Ehafo lambishi meumbo
             mwa tomwa) weakened the figurative impact.
       •	                                           Incorrect or lack of punctuation usage:  Most of the learners did not use different types of sentences,
             paragraphs and punctuation marks correctly.

2      COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

SECTION A:


1      This question was considerably a popular choice for many learners:
       “Konima         youlefimbo         eshi         nda         kala         ndihe         po         pomukunda,         onda         alukila,         nonda         mona         nghee         natango
       ovahongwa      tava,      hongelwa      koshi      yomuti      wakula      onghalo      oyo      ya      faafana      naanaa      naayo      twa      li      muyo.”
       Shanga  ehokololo  kombinga  yefimbo  omuhokololi a  li  mofikola  monghalo  ya  faafana  naayo  ya  tumbulwa
       metetekelo. Moshinyolwa shoye kwatela mo omaliudo ehafo nomadimbuluko efimbo olo.

       This question required effective use of memory and reflection; many failed to balance present observation with the
       past.  Emotional recollection is subtlety demanded.  Learners would often incoherently join their present observation
       with their past memories or vice versa.  Learners could not express their emotions or memories fully or in detail.
       Common weaknesses:
       Vague nostalgia of the memory of the school under a tree:  Learners used general statements about “Onda
       li    nda    hafa”    without    concrete    scenes    or    specific    objects    that    evoke    the    past.        Emotional    depth    was    lacking,    the
       reminiscence was told, not shown.

       Confused time frame of the past memories and the current observations:  Candidates often move between
       past and present awkwardly when trying to put together a memory (back in the day) compared to current observation
       (seeing the school now).  Learners often focused on the present scene without adequately developing the past
       memories.  While others did not even return to their previous school for their emotions to be evoked in order for
       them to experience nostalgia as requested by the prompt.
       Underdeveloped emotion of what the memories:  The essay states “Onda li handi kwena kehafo” rather than
       demonstrating why and how this feeling surfaced.

       Corrective advice:

•     Ovahongwa vahapu ova nyamukula eli, ashike ovanini vomuvo va nyamukula mondjila.
     •     Vahapu   vomuvo   inave   lifefifa   ve   litule   monghalo   oyo   va   pewa   kepulo,   meemhito   dihapu   ova   shanga   ashike
           omashongo okuhongelwa koshi yomuti, ngaashi oilipwedi, omutenya, omhepo, naikwao, nonande epulo ola
           hala menyamukulo laye mu kale edimba lehafo nokutyapula okuhongelwa koshi yomuti osho yo omadimbukulo
           oo nao a pumbwa okukala e na edimba lehafo.
     •     Mepulo    omu    ovahongwa    ova    teelelwa    va    nyole    momupersona    wotete    pamukalo    wokulifefifa    navamwe    ova
           nyola momupersona omutivali osho shihe li mondjila.

2    This question too was chosen by most candidates:
     Nyola oshinyolwa oshikwakundjodjomona koshi yoshipalanyole “Oudano wovashikingalo” moshinyolwa
     shoye kwatela mo onghalo yovanhu, onhele, omawi nomalinyengo opo omuleshi a faafanife naasho sha
     li tashi ningwa.

     This question appeared to be less challenging but learners failed to follow the prompts that required them to look
     at people, the setting (scene or place) and the sounds at this particular music event.  Many learners’ attention was
     fixed    on    speaking    about    the    performers    and    what    they    are    well    known    for    rather    than    describing    the    event    and
     following the prompts to speak about the people at the event and all the other aspects that make up the entire
     question.
     Common weaknesses:

     Over-reliance on labeling of the music show:  Writing “it was loud” or “the crowd was big” without supplying
     evidence.
     Ignoring spatial description at the music show:  Failure to place the reader in the venue (where the stage is,
     the light, the smell).

     Corrective advice:
     Ovalongwa vahapu ova kufa po epulo eli vo ove li nyamukula nawa.  Ovahonga okwa li va teelelwa va kwatele mo
     oupendulifimadiladilo ngaashi:

     Onghalo yovanhu, onhele, omawi nomalinyengo, opo omuleshi a faafanife naasho sha li tashi ningwa, oihopanenwa:
     •     Onhele:  Oukoshoki, omatuwa, okuya mo, nomafutilo pomuvelo, omalamba, omambako, oikulya, oikunwa
           nosho tuu.
     •     Ovanhu:  Omaliudo avo, omidjalo, omalihumbato ava nosho tuu.
     •     Omawi:  Omaweelelo mokule, eemwilwa, eenghuwo dehafo, omakuwililo nosho tuu.
     •     Omalinyengo:  Engungumano, emboboloko lovanhu, elandulafano, eendanisa, omalwoodi, ovanhu tava denge
           eemhadi pedu, okupandula/eemhandu.

     Use description of sound at the music show as an anchor:  Start with a specific sound and expand outward to
     physical details.
     Map the music scene visually:  For instance, encourage learners to describe the venue imaginatively in their
     writing — entrance, stage, audience, exit points — and then use spatial language.

     Layer sensory details at the music show:      Combine   sights   (lights),   smells   (dust   and   specific   food   available),
     tactile sensations (vibration through feet) and social cues (how the crowd moved).

3    Candidates who chose this question did not do justice to the question:
     Owa talela po omaumbo avali ovakwanedimo voye omafimbo a yooloka, ovakwanedimo vomeumbo limwe
     ova li va wanenwa kwaasho ve na, omanga ovakwenedimo vomeumbo likwao va li ovanalwisho nove hole
     omaliko.        Nyola    oinyolwa    ivali    oikwakundjodjomona    ya    yoolokafana,    pokati    (koitya    250    -    300)        kukeshe
     oshinyolwa    kombinga    yokukala    kwoye    momaumbo    aa    avali    moulefimbo    wetalelepo    loye.        Moshinyolwa
     shoye kwatela mo omalihumbato nomaukwatyaavo.

     The  challenge  is  that  the  question  required  nuanced  characterization  (creating  a  specific  set  of  character  for  the
     different families while focusing on their behaviours, separately), parallel structure (creating a credible opposite of
     the other), avoidance of moralizing (learners may lapse into sermonizing rather than showing behaviour through
     scenes   by   linking   it   back   to   what   they   personally   find   right   or   wrong   but   may   not   be   generally   viewed   as   such),
     and subtlety in comparison (comparing the one writing or piece to the other without noticeably appearing so).  The
     requirement to create believable contrasts without resorting to clichés (common and widely known norms that are
     reflected daily) is unavoidable in such a question.
     Many learners who chose this question did not possess the ability to show that the one family was content with
     that they had and that the other family was greedy.  The learners’ focus was on the good or bad behaviour of either
     family without following the prompts correctly to expose their content or greed through their behaviour and speech.

Common weaknesses:
     Moralising tone when referring to the two families:  Learners lapse into sermonising rather than showing
     behaviour through scenes.  They would preach about a certain thing that was done or not done by a specific family
     member rather than focusing on showing their behavior.

     Stereotyping of the two families:  One family becomes an exaggeration (saints’ vs villains) without realistic
     motivations.  They claim that these families are bad with very little to no evidence shown in their writing.
     Poor contrast technique in comparing the two families:  Many learners listed good or bad qualities and
     immoralities instead of weaving contrast through parallel incidents.

     Ovahongwa vanini ova hoolola epulo eli ashike inave li nyamukula nawa.  Oitwa ya etwa kovahongwa nai kale ya
