1.    GENERAL COMMENTS

Based on previous year’s (2024) question paper 2, this year’s question paper seems to be fair as per candidates’
responses.  Different responses from candidates were fair and indeed good, though there were some candidates who
could not answer some questions they chose correctly.

Generally, candidates need to be exposed to a variety of sources such as narrative writing, descriptive writing and
argumentative writing, because the examination paper is assessed in those areas.  This will help candidates to know
the structure, tone and logic demanded in each essay.

This year (2025) candidates repeated the same answering method of not capturing the main keywords (verbs) in
each question before attempting to answer them.  Through the help of teachers, candidates are advised to read to
comprehend any question they opt for to prepare better, so that the emphasis of their writing should be based on their
competence in answering the question.

In addition, most of the candidates have a problem with punctuation marks, spelling or using vocabulary in the correct
way, therefore it affected the grammar and structure of their writing.  All that must be taught thoroughly to answer the
question properly.  A good example of wrong vocabulary usage:  in part A question 4 (see the question paper 2, 2025),
candidates were expected to write about how a successful team was defeated. Vanona kuna kuuyunga asi:  “Tupu

The length of their writing needs more improvement; some candidates could not write 500 to 600 /250 to 300 words

1     GENERAL COMMENTS

This was the third external examination under the new syllabus.  88 candidates were entered for this examination.
During the first year there were 65, then 56 candidates.  There were 11 centres that offered German Foreign Language
on AS level, only two centres had more than 10 candidates, thus 57 candidates’ speaking tests were moderated.  The
same mark schemes as the previous year were used.

In general, it was established by the moderators that this year examiners awarded marks for the presentation (Part A)
correctly but were still more generous when awarding marks for Parts B and C of the speaking examination.  It must be
mentioned that teachers were generally forthcoming and friendly during the speaking examination.

Overall, the quality of the recordings was clear.  Teachers and candidates could be heard equally clearly.  Fewer centres
presented the speaking examination with the teacher ’s voice closer to the microphone than that of the candidate.  This is
appreciated by the moderators, as the candidate’s speaking ability is tested.  There were less background noises on the
recordings, which was also appreciated by the moderators.  It needs to be mentioned that candidates need to present
some statistics, to show that they have researched the topic and they should compare Namibia with some other country
where German is spoken, such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria or Lichtenstein, or just present the topic about one of
these countries.  The mentioning of statistics was generally done this year.

When teachers conduct the speaking examination, they do not have to address their candidates in the “Höflichkeitsform
Sie”,   nor   the   other   way   around.      They   address   them   the   same   way   as   they   would   when   teaching   them,   which   could
include the name of the candidate and “du”.  The candidates may answer with the name of the teacher and “du” as well.
Teachers   are   advised   to   stick   to   one   format   of   addressing   and   not   hop   between   the   two   possibilities   of   informal   and
formal.  Fewer examiners hopped between the two forms this year.

Teachers     should     mention     when     they     switch     from     one     section     to     the     next,     such     as     we     have     completed     Part    A,     the
questions for Part B are as follows.  For the 2025 oral examination this was adhered to by all the centers.

It  is  good  to  mention  at  the  end  of  the  recording  of  each  candidate  “end  of  sample”.    Teachers  also  must  record  only
once all the information about the centre and the examination have taken place.  It does not have to be repeated at the
beginning   of   each   candidate’s   oral.      Regarding   the   beforementioned   aspects,   examiners   also   adhered   to   the   advice
given in last year ’s report.

In future, teachers should mention the general topic, such as Medien and then the specific topic on which the candidate
does     his     or     her     presentation.         The     specific     topic     should     be     of     a     conflicting     nature,     or     the     candidate     should     make     a
provocative statement and then explore that in his or her presentation, such as “Social media only influence teenagers
negatively.”           The      comparison      part      should      not      be      contained      in      the      title.            Most      centres      this      year      only      had      prepared
presentations on the general topics.

When     a     candidate     asks     a     question     to     be     repeated,     he     or     she     should     not     be     presented     with     a     completely     different
question by the teacher.  Teachers may rephrase the original question, but should refrain from long, elaborate questions.

2     COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

The speaking examination for the Foreign Language German AS learners consists of three parts.

Every year there are                                                                       five general topics available for the Foreign Language German AS learners and they then choose
one   of   the   topics   to   do   their   presentation   on,   going   into   more   detail   on   the   chosen   topic.     Thus,   there   is   no   question
paper      available,      only      a      mark      scheme      for      this      specific      examination.           This      year      all      five      general      topics      were      spoken
about,    the    most    popular    one    being    “Arbeit    und    Freizeit    /    Entspannung”,    and    the    least    used    was    “wissenschaftlicher
und medizinischer Fortschritt”.  It must be mentioned here that 14 candidates prepared presentations about seemingly
random topics, not taking into consideration the five prescribed topics of that specific year.

Part A is a presentation by each learner which should not be longer than three minutes, but also not shorter than two
and   a   half   minutes.      Overall,   this   was   not   a   problem   although   some   learners   were   allowed   to   present   for   almost   four
minutes.    It  should  be  mentioned  that  three  minutes  are  sufficient  and  that  learners  may  be  stopped.    The  rest  of  the
presentation, should there be some parts not presented, could be used for the second part, where questions are asked
about the presentation of the learner.  At the end of the presentation the teacher should announce the end of this part
or introduce the second part.

Learners    must    make    some    reference    to    a    German-speaking    country.        Some    statistics    should    be    presented    to    show
that   the   candidate   has   done   some   research   on   the   topic.      Most   centres   accommodated   this   successfully   during   this
examination    session.       Learners   may    make    use    of  AI   but    should    make    the    contents    of    their    presentation    “their    own”.
How AI constructs texts, was used by some candidates as is.  Learners should be made aware of the fact that they start
their presentation with a controversial statement.  How to present a topic should be practised during the Grade 12 year.

If a learner asks a question in this section already, the teacher should answer the question and not ignore it or prompt
the   candidate   to   continue   without   answering   the   candidate’s   question.      The   marks   given   for   questioning   then   will   go
towards Part B.

Teachers should ask “new”questions on the topic presented.  Questions should be formulated to explore the presentation
on a wider level, or on parts which the learner has not been able to present due to the time constraint.

Part  B  is  the  first  conversation.    Its  contents  should  cover  the  topic  of  Part A.   The  teacher  thus  needs  to  be  prepared
to ask the learner questions and give enough time for the learner to answer.  It is very important that in Part B as well
as in Part C the learner needs to ask the teacher                                                                                                             at least two questions.  Should the learner not do this close to the
end   of   each   conversation,   the   teacher   must   prompt   the   learner   to   do   so.      Questions   asked   by   the   teacher   should
be    on  AS    level,    specifically    asking    for    reasons    and    explanations.       This    part    of    the    speaking    examination    should    be
spontaneous and not learned off by heart before the time.  It should not be longer than seven minutes and not shorter
than 6 minutes.

Part    C is the second conversation which should also last about                         seven    minutes    and    not    be    shorter    than    6    minutes.
Altogether the speaking examination should thus be close to 17 minutes long, but NOT longer than 20 minutes.  The
learner needs to ask the teacher at least two questions in this section as well.  Should the learner not do this close to the
end of this part of the conversation, the teacher must prompt the learner to do so.  If only one question is asked during
each   conversation,   the   maximum   mark   for   this   category   is   3   marks   out   of   a   possible   five.      When   no   questions   were
asked, no marks can be obtained.   In both conversations  the  questions that are  put to the teacher  should have to
do with the topic being discussed.  Teachers should be aware that even though learners must ask them questions,
they as teachers                                                                           should keep their answers concise.  It is a speaking examination for the learners.

In Part C questions on the other four topics for that specific year are supposed to be asked.  The teacher does not
have to cover all four topics.  Two could be sufficient as well, for that matter.  Neither in Part B nor in Part C the answers
to possible questions should be learned off by heart.  Both conversations should be spontaneous.  Questions asked in
this part should be on AS level (and not on O level).  Many examiners teach both grades and thus are familiar with the
topics of O level, but must at the same time be aware of the difference in levels between Grades 11 and 12.

Actions needing attention and suggestions to examiners

Just   as   for   the   essay   paper,   learners   need   to   make   use   of   the   correct   phrases   when   expressing   an   opinion:   meiner
Meinung nach, ich denke, ich meine, was halten Sie davon wie denken Sie                                                                                darüber, was ist Ihre Meinung dazu (NOT
darüber) u.  Ä (NOT in meiner Meinung, in deiner Meinung nach – no preposition at the beginning for the latter).  Another
phrase that needs attention:  Das hängt von … ab (NOT das davon abhängen).  The correct form of verbs in the Perfekt
should also be practised as from Grade 10, e.g. essen – gegessen (NOT ge-essen).  The difference between Uhr and
Stunde needs to be clear, also when to use which word in which context.  The people living in Namibia are Namibier in
German, NOT Namibianer.

When replying in the warm-up, many candidates chose the wrong congruency:  Wie geht es Frau? It must be: Wie geht
es Ihnen or Wie geht es Ihnen,                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           Frau followed by the surname of the teacher?  Also, ich wohne                                                                            bei meiner Mutter or
ich wohne mit meinen Geschwistern zusammen bei meinen Eltern and NOT:  ich wohne mit meiner Mutter, which is a
direct translation from their mother tongue.  Einkaufszentrum is the beautiful German word for Mall.

Key Message:
Learners should ensure that they understand that Question 5 requires them to summarise both texts in their own words,
whereby problems and solutions are to be covered regarding pollution and environmental issues.

1    GENERAL COMMENTS

Candidates in general performed less successfully than in the previous year, where they wrote the NSSCAS level
examinations for the second time in Foreign Language German.  This shows, that teachers should receive advice from
a training workshop again to prepare their learners more thoroughly.

Most candidates tried to use their own words for answering the questions and it rarely happened that random sections
from the text were copied.  However, some candidates just reshuffled the words from the text to create an answer which
resulted in sentences which did not make sense at all.

Learners  should  be  made  aware,  that  due  to  the  fixed  time  of  1  hour  45  minutes,  learners  have  no  time  to  write  their
answers in pencil first.  The instructions are clear on the front page to write in dark blue or black pen.

Questions 3 and 4 require structured sentences, not abbreviated bullet point type of answers.

Question 5 requires a short piece of writing to be structured as an essay.  Again, abbreviated bullet points do not give
credit to essay expectations.

2    COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS
     Question 1

     In this part of the paper, learners are given five synonyms for words from the text and then have to find matching
     words    from    that    text.      All    words    can    be    found    in    the    first    paragraph    of    the    first    text    and    have    to    fit    into    the    text
     appropriately.  The words are in sequence in that paragraph and can be identified according to their parts of speech
     (Wortarten).

     In this year, many candidates could not master this question well especially because they disregarded that the
     parts of speech of the given word can guide them, e.g., a noun requires a synonym noun again.

     Where candidates copied the word incorrectly, when they wrote “verursacht” for “gemacht “with a capital “V”, that
     answer was not credited.

     Learners often can be guided by the ending of a word as in “akutes” which shows that this adjective ends with “es”
     and the answer “drängendes” also ends with “es”.  A plural noun must have a plural noun as a synonym again.

     Question 2

     In this part of the paper, learners are required to rephrase sentences from text 1 to test their grammatical knowledge.
     More candidates compared to the previous year found this exercise very challenging and about 80 % of the
     candidates could not obtain any marks.  A few learners could obtain full marks, but it was obvious that they were
     of German Mother tongue background.  A few learners knew how to convert the direct speech “meine Tomaten”
     to indirect speech “ihre Tomaten”, while some did not know the female possessive pronoun and used the male
     pronoun “seine”.  Learners should be reminded only to write the answers in the open spaces instead of copying
     the whole sentence.  They are not awarded any marks, if they make a spelling mistake anywhere in the copied
     sentence even if the requested answer phrase would have been correct.

     Question 3

     In this part of the paper, learners have to answer comprehension questions based on the first text.  15 points are
     awarded for content, while 5 extra marks are available for the quality of language used. If learners lift information
     directly from the text, they cannot obtain language marks and they may lose marks for not demonstrating full
     understanding of the text.  Learners should not randomly reshuffle the words, which may lead to sentences which
     do   not   make   sense,   such   as   “Musst   jeder   verwendet   ein   Baum   nachgepflanzt   werden”   or   “Durch   die   Einnahme

und Verdauung des Menschen in die Abwässer.”  By taking in and devouring of people into the sewerage waters.

(a)   Many candidates obtained full marks, while some candidates did not understand that household
      appliances are made from plastic, glass or metal or could not understand that these materials are not
      easily utilised for bio degradable purposes.

(b)   Only     a     few     candidates     could     not     find     the     examples     for     using     natural     resources:     “Holz     für     Möbel”
      and   “Pflanzenfasern   für   Kleidung”.      Some   candidates,   however,   forgot,   that   questions   are   asked   in
      sequence within the text and they interchanged the answers of 3b with 3c.  In that case, the answers
      were not credited.

(c)   Many candidates obtained all 3 marks.  The information of the reason as to why trees should be
      replanted was added to the mark scheme, because many candidates wrote about that explanation,
      instead of “umweltbewusst vorgehen”.  Only one of those two pieces of information was credited,
      however,   to   add   to   the   other   two   pieces   of   information:         “Bäume   nachpflanzen”   and   “Ackergebiete
      nicht     einseitig     bepflanzen”.          With     mother     tongue     background     it     was     possible     for     one     candidate     to
      replace “einseitig” with “Man sollte Ackergebiete mehrseitig bepflanzen”.  Again, when two questions
      relate to one longer paragraph, then the two questions which relate to it are in sequence.

(d)   Many candidates obtained full marks.  Some candidates did not clarify clearly, that due to population
      explosion “humans” or their living areas “Wohngebiete” take over areas that were once inhabited
      by        plants        and        animals        resulting        in        random        reshuffling.                For        example,        “Es        ist        ihre        Wohngebiete
      übernehmen die Gegenden.”

(e)   Some candidates reshuffled the sentences to write sentences that do not make sense.  In that case,
      instead of “bei der Herstellung von Medikamenten“, they wrote „Bei der Herstellung und Verdauung
      des Menschen“.  By the construction and devouring of humans...

(f)   Many candidates only gave an example of how harmful chemicals can enter the human body, namely
      through the pores when playing football on a pitch which has been watered with contaminated water.
      Few       candidates       identified       the       two       other       facts,       namely       that       tomatoes       can       become       contaminated
      with  chemicals  when  watered  with  semi-purified  water  and  people  then  eat  the  tomatoes  containing
      harmful chemicals.
Question 4

In  this  part  of  the  paper,  learners  have  to  answer  comprehension  questions  based  on  the  second  text.    15  points
are   awarded   for   content,   while   5   extra   marks   are   available   for   the   quality   of   language   use.    Again,   if   learners   lift
information directly from the text, they cannot obtain language marks and they may lose marks for not demonstrating
full understanding of the text.

Many candidates struggled to rephrase the answers to relate to the expectation of the questions.  Some candidates
randomly    copied    phrases    from    the    text    and    reshuffled    the    words    to    write    a    piece    of    writing    which    did    not    make
sense at all.  As such, they lost content marks and language marks.

Some candidates wrote abbreviated bullet points where the meaning was not conveyed properly.  Short but
complete sentences assist in structuring a clear message in the answer.

(a)   Many        candidates        obtained        the        full        2        marks        for        this        question.               A        few        candidates        reshuffled        the
      sentences      randomly.            Examples      are:            “Man      kann      bepflastert      ganze      Flächen      mit      Solarkollektoren
      oder      Windrädern,      als      man      kann      Wasserturbinen      gebrauchen      um      Elektizität      zu      erzeugen      und      auf
      Solaranlagen setzen.“ „Die Menschen können alle Dächer auf Solaranlagen setzen.“  The people can
      put all roofs on solar panels.

(b)   The    majority    of    candidates    scored    both    possible    marks,    but    again    the    same    candidates    reshuffled
      sentences randomly or used abbreviated bullet points.

(c)   This  question  required  4  possible  facts  to  be  identified  and  many  candidates  gained  all  four  marks.
      By using compound sentences and pronouns, some candidates gave ambiguous answers where it
      was not clear whether they were referring to insects or birds.  An example of reshuffling randomly is:
      “Auf natürliche Weise bekämpfen man muss Insekten bei der Bestäubung und außerdem Nahrung für
      unterschiedliche Vögel sind.  “By natural means you must fight against insects which are pollinating
      plants and at the same time are food for different birds.

Some candidates did not pay attention to spelling, which could change the meaning of the word
      completely and instead of “Man soll verschiedene Blumen wachsen lassen”  You should let different
      flowers grow, they wrote “Man soll verschiedene Blumen waschen lassen” which means You should
      let different flowers be washed.

(d)   3  answers  were  expected.    Many  candidates  did  not  realise  that  to  use  “Pfandflaschen”  was  part  of
      the answer.  They also were not credited if they did not clarify why people should carry containers
      with them, namely that they would use them for shopping, as in “Man soll eigene Behälter für Waren
      mitnehmen.”  The third information related to “unverpacktes Obst kaufen” oder zumindest “unverpackte
      Waren kaufen“.  Many candidates wrote „Man soll unverpackt kaufen“, which means one should buy
      unwrapped, which implies that people might have to appear unwrapped.  That information could not
      be credited.

(e)   This question required 4 answers.  Most candidates could obtain at least 3 out of 4 marks.

Question 5

This question required an argumentative essay approach, whereby the arguments for the problems of pollution and
possible solutions to the situations should be taken from both texts.

More candidates than last year wrote an introduction to the text.  However, those introductions were too long.
A    suitable    short    introduction    could    be    adapted    from    the    instruction:        “Es    gibt    viele    Umweltprobleme,    aber    auch
Lösungen dazu.”

Very few candidates wrote paragraphs for the problems and solutions to rectify or combat environmental issues.
Many candidates did not relate to the texts but randomly wrote their own version without stating that it was their own
opinion.  Own opinions must be clearly stated as, “Meiner Meinung nach… - Ich denke, dass …,”

To gain marks for their own opinion, the candidates could easily relate to the advice given, that they should clarify
which solutions to environmental issues could be applied to the situation in Namibia.

Two candidates did not write anything at all.  Learners can be guided by some informational details, which they
have covered in the questions 3 and 4 at least to attempt to answer question 5.  Any answer beyond the word limit
cannot be credited, thus, it is advisable for learners to include that own opinions within the written text.

Candidates who copied and reshuffled random phrases in Question 4 did the same in Question 5 and their answers
made no sense so could not be credited.

Some candidates gave their shortened answers in the form of bullet points, which cannot be evaluated as an
argumentative essay approach.  Random copying of text phrases can also not be credited.

Many candidates ended their argumentative essay with their personal response to give a clear indication that they
had taken note of section (b) in the question, but many candidates did not elaborate on their opinion to be credited
with   5   marks.      Most   candidates’   own   opinions,   however,   were   clearly   stated   and   gave   the   impression   of   a   clear
stance to the theme.
A few candidates constructed their whole essay around the situation of Namibia, thus ignored Section A of
the     question,     which     counted     10     marks.         That     also     affected     the     language     mark,     which     takes     both     sections     into
consideration.

General  Teaching Advice:

Learners should be made familiar with the words “ der Vorteil und der Nachteil” for argumentative Essays.

It is advisable to teach the learners fixed phrases, such as
•    Der erste Vorteil…
•    Ein weiterer Vorteil ...,               Ein weiterer Aspekt ...
•    Zusätzlich kann man sagen, dass ...,               dazu kann man ergänzen, dass ...
•    Dagegen spricht, dass ... ,                Als Gegenargument sagen viele / manche, dass ...
•    Nicht nur ...., aber auch ...
•    Zum Schluss kann man sagen, dass ...               Zusammenfassend kann man sagen, dass ...
•    Meiner Meinung nach ...               Ich denke, dass ...               Ich finde, dass ...
•    Learners should be taught once more the difference between :
      “für” und “vor”                “wenn“ und „als“ und „anstatt“               „weil“ und „wann“

•     In German you use articles for sentences, unlike English, where you do write, “People believe that meat is
           unhealthy.”  In German: “Die Menschen sollten natürliche Düngemittel einsetzen.”
     •     Umlaute have a function in German, because they change the sound of a vocal.  It must be “sparen” not
           “spären”, “bedroht” not “bedröht”.  Many candidates used single words from the text to then spell them with
           or without Umlaut to either end up with a changed meaning or no meaning at all.
     •     The comma is in front of the conjunction, which is the same sentence structure in English, Afrikaans or then
           German.
     •     The word “or” is written without the “r” in German as “         oder”.
     •     Learners should be able to conjugate “haben”, “sein” und “werden” and Modal verbs at this stage, as well as
           be able to know how to detect singular and plural nouns to be able to conjugate the verbs accordingly.

Thank you to all the teachers for putting in so much dedication to prepare the learners for the NSSCAS examinations.

GENERAL COMMENTS

This was the third written external examination under the new syllabus.  82 candidates wrote this examination; thus 82
essays were marked.  To mark the essays, the same marking scheme as the previous year was used.

Candidates coped well with all five topics, although it must be emphasised that candidates should discuss the specific
topic, and not just the general one.

COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS

In the Writing Paper, all the topics are either discursive or argumentative.  During the year in which the Foreign Language
German AS level is taught, the teachers are presented with five topics, as can be seen below.  For the essays however,
a     specific     aspect     under     each     topic     needs     to    be     addressed.         This     is     the     title     of    each     essay     that     is     to     be     written     on.
Learners should write the specific title of the topic on top of the page, NOT the GENERAL TOPIC.  Therefore, it can be
said, that some candidates wrote about the topic instead of on the specific title, or only ever so slightly touched on the
title.  If a candidate did not at all write about what is asked in the title, then no marks can be awarded for Content and
only some marks for Language.  As a teacher the adequate row in the Mark Scheme still must reflect authentic German.
If the essay contains other European grammatical structures or vocabulary, it definitely influences both the Content and
the Language mark.

Writing an essay consisting of 250 – 400 words needs to be practised.  The availability of more lines to write the essay
on helped the candidates to produce better argumentative or discursive essays this year as well.  Blank pages may be
used  for  planning.    Candidates  who  do  their  planning,  deliver  a  better-quality  essay.    It  is  essential  that  candidates  do
that in their final examination, as the mark scheme awards marks for a clear structure: introduction, paragraphs and a
conclusion. In the introduction candidates should mention the title.  The conclusion should contain a clear point of view.

Foreign Language German AS learners may give their opinion in the introduction, but still need to write a proper
conclusion.

The following topics were given to the candidates, of which one had to be answered.

Umweltverschmutzung

1.    „Keiner in meinem Dorf kümmert sich um Recycling.  Deshalb tragen wir Menschen selbst die Schuld für
      die Zerstörung unserer Umwelt.“
      Diskutieren Sie diese Aussage.

Umwelt / meine Umgebung


2.    „Wasserknappheit ist eine Folge der Klimakrise“, behauptet ein Klimaaktivist.  „Dies ist aber nicht das
      einzige Problem zum Thema Klimawandel.“
      Setzen Sie sich mit dieser Behauptung kritisch auseinander.

Arbeit und Freizeit


3.    „Ich freue mich darauf, bald nur noch vier Tage die Woche zur Arbeit gehen zu müssen“, meint ein junger
      Geschäftsführer.
      Nehmen Sie zu dieser Aussage Stellung.

Wissenschaftlicher und medizinischer Fortschritt

4.    Genveränderung ist ein Eingriff in die Natur. Ist Genforschung moralisch vertretbar?
      Äußern Sie sich kritisch zu dieser Fragestellung.

Gleichberechtigung

5.    „Wir Menschen sind alle gleich.  Trotzdem überlegt man sich, Jungen und Mädchen wieder in getrennte Schulen
      zu schicken.“
      Erklären Sie ausführlich Ihre Meinung zu diesem Thema.

Topic 1 was the most popular topic.  31 of the 82 candidates wrote about Umweltverschmutzung.  The reading texts of
paper 2 covered this topic, thus candidates used vocabulary, information and arguments from the reading texts in their
essays.  This, however, caused the candidates occasionally to ignore the specific topic.

Topic     3     was     the     second     most     popular     topic.          22     of     the     82     candidates     wrote     about   Arbeit     und     Freizeit.          Candidates
covered the general topic more often than writing about the specific topic.  The specific topic required a discussion on a
four-day workweek.  Only single essays were successful at this discussion.

Topic 5 was the third most popular topic.  15 of the 82 candidates wrote about Gleichberechtigung.  Generally, candidates
discussed the general topic, and not the specific one.  The latter required a discussion on separating boys and girls into
different schools.  It would have been pleasing to see what the advantages and disadvantages of separate schools are,
as well as for mixed-gender schools.

Topic  2  was  chosen  by  13  of  the  82  candidates.   Although  the  general  topic  is  very  close  to  topic  1,  the  specific  topic
required   a   different   avenue.     The   specific   topic   mentioned   water   shortages   because   of   climate   change.     This   should
have    been    explored    as    well    as    other    factors    contributing    to    climate    change.        Generally,    only    the    second    part    of    the
specific topic was focused on, thus resulting in only satisfactory essays.

Topic 4, about scientific and medical progress, specifically questioning whether gene manipulation is ethical and moral,
was  chosen  by  one  candidate.   The  candidate  produced  a  well-argued  essay.    It  must  be  mentioned  that  it  was  clear
that this was a candidate with German as mother tongue background.

Some vocabulary and grammar to which the teachers should pay more attention to:
•	                                                  Only nouns are written with a capital letter in German.
•	                                                  Relativsätze, as in die Schüler, die … NOT die Schüler, was …
•	                                                  Negation, as in kein or keine NOT mit ohne
•	                                                  Steigerungen, as in klüger NOT mehr klug; which is a direct, wrong translation from English.
•     In “das größte Problem” – problem takes on the neutral definite article das, and then learners should be taught the
      correct endings of adjectives when combining definite articles, adjectives and nouns, which could be a topic for a
      workshop.
•     The  position  of  verbs  in  sentences  and  subclauses  as  well  that  Modalverben  always  go  together  with  the  Infinitiv
      form of the second verb, as in kann verursachen.
•	                                                  After linking words in German there is NO comma as in Außerdem ist der Mensch …
•	                                                  Adjectives    are written in small, and nouns are written with a                                                                                                                                                                                 capital letter as in sauberes Wasser, stabile
      Temperaturen, fossile Ressourcen.
•     „man“ conjugates the same way as “er, sie, es”, therefore it should also read “es hilft einem” (NOT es hilft man)
•     “false     friends”     should     be     avoided,     as     in     Zeit     spandieren,     correct:     verbringen,     affektieren,     correct:     beeinflussen,
      Faktoren vs. Fabriken (factories in English), wohnen vs. bleiben, wees (Afrikaans) is NOT wissen in German, Gase
      vs Gasse, alley in German, arbeiten NOT werken from Afrikaans, fokusieren correct: sich auf etwas konzentrieren
•	                                                  “ich” is written small in the middle of a sentence.
•     the difference between wenn and als
•     Sentence structures need to be practised more:
      -      …., weil ……. Verb

(b)  AOB:  Explain the components of the hydrological cycle in tropical deserts during summer.
     Comment on question
     Fairly well answered as candidates showed knowledge of the processes of a hydrological cycle, but could
     not explain how it changes in summer as well as in tropical deserts.
     Wrong answers
     Rainfall is less in summer than in winter.
     Desert rainfall is more than 1000mm in summer
     The lag time is shorter and the rising limb is gentle
     Correct answers
     Evaporation:  the intense heat in tropical deserts during summer leads to high evaporation rates.  The sun’s
     energy causes the water on the surface, such as rivers, lakes or even soil moisture, to evaporate and transform
     into water vapor.
     Transpiration:  vegetation in tropical deserts, although sparse, undergoes transpiration, wherein plants
     release water vapor through their leaves.  This contributes to the overall moisture in the atmosphere.
     Condensation:  as the water vapour rises in the atmosphere, it cools down, leading to condensation.  This
     process forms clouds, especially during the late afternoon or evening when the temperatures drop.
     Precipitation:  in tropical deserts during summer, precipitation is relatively low. However, occasional rain
     showers or thunderstorms may occur due to the convective activity generated by the intense heat and rapid
     heating of the land surface.  These rain showers are typically short-lived but can provide temporary relief to
     the arid environment.
     Infiltration:  when precipitation occurs, a portion of it penetrates the ground, a process known as infiltration.
     The sandy soils found in tropical deserts have good drainage capacity, which allows water to percolate into
     the underground aquifers.
     Runoff:  due to the limited vegetation cover and the porous nature of desert soils, the rate of surface runoff is
     high in tropical deserts.  This means that a significant portion of the precipitation quickly flows over the surface,
     rather than being absorbed by the ground.
     Groundwater recharge:  in tropical deserts, where water availability is limited, groundwater plays a crucial
     role.  The infiltration of water into the ground helps recharge the underground water reserves, sustaining the
     oasis and providing water for plants, animals and human communities.
     Evapotranspiration:  The combination of evaporation and transpiration, known as evapotranspiration, is
     a vital stage in the hydrological cycle.  In tropical deserts during summer, with high temperatures and low
     humidity, evapotranspiration rates can be quite significant, resulting in the loss of water from the surface back
     into the atmosphere.                                                                                                               [6]

     Accept other relevant answers

     Any 3/6 explanations – 1 explanation developed well can gain an extra mark for development.

     Suggested improvement

     influenced    in    each    season.       Teachers    should    also    clearly    explain    the    differences    between    the    hydrological
     cycle and the hydrographs.

(c)  AOB (3) AOD (7):  To what extent do you agree that the modification of the hydrological cycle
     is caused by human activities?
     Comment on question
     Well answered
     Candidates could make decisions, as they could evaluate how human activities or physical factors modify
     the hydrological cycle. Many learners could score at least seven marks.

     Correct answers
     Ideas such as

     Agree to a large extent/agrees
     Dam construction:  humans modify the hydrological cycle by building dams across rivers, which can control
     the flow of water, store water in reservoirs and release water when needed for various purposes such as
     irrigation, drinking water supply or hydroelectric power generation.
      Deforestation:  the removal of trees and vegetation alters the hydrological cycle by reducing evapotranspiration,
      which is the process of water vapour being released into the atmosphere through both plant transpiration and

evaporation from the soil.  This results in decreased rainfall, disrupted precipitation patterns and changes in
runoff dynamics.
Urbanization:  the expansion of urban areas and construction of impervious surfaces, such as roads, buildings
and parking lots modify the hydrological cycle by reducing the amount of water that infiltrates into the ground.
This leads to increased surface runoff, decreased groundwater recharge and increased likelihood of flooding.
Irrigation:  humans modify the hydrological cycle by using water from freshwater sources, such as rivers
or  underground  aquifers,  to  irrigate  crops.   This  increases  the  amount  of  water  evaporated  from  agricultural
fields, resulting in altered evapotranspiration rates and potentially affecting regional rainfall patterns.
Climate change:  human-induced climate change is altering the hydrological cycle on a global scale.
Increased greenhouse gas emissions from human activities are leading to rising global temperatures, which
in turn affect precipitation patterns, evaporation rates and the overall water cycle.  This can result in changes
in  rainfall  intensity,  shifts  in  the  timing  and  distribution  of  rainfall,  as  well  as  increased  frequency  of  extreme
weather events such as droughts and floods.
Agrees to a low extent/disagrees
Natural Climate change:  rising global temperatures due to climate change can lead to changes in precipitation
patterns and the melting of glaciers as well as ice sheets.  These changes can modify the hydrological cycle
by altering the timing and amount of water availability.
Natural disasters:  events such as hurricanes, floods and droughts can significantly impact the hydrological
cycle.    For  example,  hurricanes  can  cause  heavy  rainfall  and  flooding,  whereas  droughts  can  lead  to  water
scarcity and decreased river flow.
Volcanic eruptions:  volcanic eruptions can release large amounts of ash and gases into the atmosphere,
which can affect rainfall patterns.  The ash particles can act as cloud condensation nuclei, potentially leading
to increased rainfall, while volcanic gases like sulfur dioxide can form aerosols that reflect sunlight and lead to
cooling, impacting evaporation rates.
Earthquakes and landslides:                these        natural        phenomena        can        alter        the        flow        of        water        by        changing        the
topography of the land, creating new pathways for water or blocking existing ones.  This can result in increased
or decreased runoff, affecting the overall balance of the hydrological cycle.
Erosion and sedimentation:  natural processes like erosion and sedimentation can modify watercourses or
river channels.  The movement of sediments can alter river flow patterns and affect the distribution as well as
the availability of water, thus impacting the hydrological cycle.

Agrees to a certain extent/ agrees and disagrees

(b)  AOB:  Explain the local daytime energy budget in terms of input and output analysis.
     Comment on question
     Poorly answered; many candidates could explain insolation as input and terrestrial radiations as output, but
     could not explain other processes.  Candidates were able to score at least two marks.

     Correct answers

     The input of energy in the daytime energy budget can come from several sources:
     Incoming solar radiation:  the primary source of energy input during the daytime is the Sun.  Solar
     radiation provides the Earth with heat and light energy.
     Human activities:  human activities can also contribute to the input of energy in the form of artificial light
     sources, such as streetlights and buildings.
     Latent heat transfers:  when a substance changes from one phase to another, such as from solid to
     liquid or liquid to gas, energy is released in the form of latent heat adding energy to the daytime budget. An
     example would be when water condenses and changes from a gas to a liquid, it releases latent heat into its
     surroundings, causing the surrounding area to warm up.
     The output of energy refers to the ways in which energy is released or transferred from the local
     area:
     Terrestrial radiation:  the Earth’s surface absorbs a portion of the incoming solar radiation and re-emits it
     as long wave radiation or infrared radiation.  This terrestrial radiation is an important output of energy, as it
     helps to cool the Earth’s surface.
     Evaporation:  energy is also transferred from the local area through the process of evaporation.  When
     water evaporates, it takes energy from the surroundings, causing a cooling effect.
     Convection:  heat is transported vertically in the atmosphere through convection. Warm air rises, carrying
     energy away from the surface, while cooler air sinks, transferring energy back to the surface.
     Reflection and scattering:  some of the incoming solar radiation is reflected or scattered back to space
     without being absorbed by the Earth’s surface.  This reflects a loss of energy from the local area.

     Accept other relevant answers

Suggested improvement

(c)  AOB (3) AOD (7):  To what extent do you agree that difficulties experienced by governments
     in population control policies to decrease the birth rate can be overcome?
     Comment on question
     Fairly well answered, as candidates were able to score at least five marks.  The majority tried to use a case
     study of Chinese one child policy, but could not make a thorough evaluation of how the challenges of the
     Chinese policy could or could not be overcome.

     Correct answer
     Ideas such as:

     ways to overcome difficulties in decreasing the birth rate:
     comprehensive education and awareness programs:  a successful population control policy
     should prioritize educating the population on the importance of controlling birth rates and the potential
     consequences of overpopulation.  By raising awareness about the benefits of having smaller families,
     providing information on contraception options and debunking common myths, people can make informed
     decisions about family planning.
     accessible and affordable contraception:  improving access to contraception is crucial in reducing
     birth rates.  Governments can work to ensure that contraceptives are affordable, widely available and
     easily accessible, particularly in rural areas where healthcare services may be limited.  This could involve

establishing clinics, training healthcare workers and subsidizing the cost of contraception.
Incentives and support for small families:  offering financial incentives and support to families who choose to
have fewer children can be effective in reducing birth rates.  These incentives could include cash rewards, tax
benefits,  educational  scholarships  or  preferential  access  to  housing  or  healthcare  services.    Such  measures
can help alleviate financial concerns and encourage families to opt for smaller family sizes.
Improved healthcare and child survival rates:  high birth rates are often associated with high infant and child
mortality rates.  By investing in better healthcare infrastructure, access to healthcare services and improving
child survival rates, parents may feel more confident in having fewer children.  This can also help address the
socio-cultural factors that contribute to high birth rates, such as the need for additional children for old age
support.
Advocacy and partnership:                            a              successful              population              control              policy              requires              collaboration              between
governments,   NGOs,   community   leaders   and   other   stakeholders.      Governments   can   partner   with   non-profit
organizations, educational institutions and community leaders to advocate for family planning as well as birth
control initiatives.  This collaborative approach ensures that diverse perspectives and expertise are brought
together to create effective strategies to overcome potential resistance or cultural barriers.
Monitoring and evaluation:  regular monitoring and evaluation of population control programmes are
essential    to    ensure    their    success.        Governments    should    collect    accurate    data    on    birth    rates,    contraceptive
usage and the impact of the policy.  This data can be used to assess the effectiveness of the programme,
identify areas for improvement and make necessary adjustments to the policy.
Addressing cultural and societal norms:  population control policies may face challenges due to cultural or
societal norms that prioritize large families.  It is important for governments to engage with local communities
and  address  these  norms  sensitively,  by  highlighting  the  benefits  of  smaller  families  both  for  individuals  and
society as a whole.  Engaging religious and community leaders in supporting the policy can also help overcome
resistance or misconduct.

Why can difficulties not be overcome in decreasing birth rates?
Cultural and societal norms:  in some cultures, having a large number of children is considered desirable
and even necessary for various reasons, such as ensuring family lineage, providing support in old age or
contributing to the labour force.  These ingrained beliefs can make it challenging to change attitudes towards
smaller family sizes and decrease birth rates.
Lack of access to contraception and family planning services:  in many regions, particularly in
developing countries, there is limited availability and accessibility of contraception methods and family
planning services.  This lack of access can hinder efforts to control birth rates and lead to higher fertility
rates.
Religious and ethical considerations:  religious beliefs and ethical considerations can influence
attitudes towards birth control and family planning.  Some religions discourage or even forbid the use of
contraception, leading to larger family sizes and difficulty in decreasing birth rates in communities where
religious adherence is strong.
Lack of education and awareness:  in some areas, there is a lack of education and awareness about the
benefits of smaller family sizes and the importance of family planning.  This can contribute to higher birth
rates as individuals may not be aware of the available options or the long-term consequences of having
many children.
Economic and social factors:  poverty, lack of economic opportunities, and inadequate social security
systems can also contribute to higher birth rates.  In such situations, having more children may be seen as
a means of ensuring economic support or a safety net for the future.  Without addressing these underlying
issues, it can be challenging to overcome difficulties in reducing birth rates.

HISTORY

           8234
        Paper 1



GENERAL COMMENTS
The question paper was moderately difficult. Most learners prepared well across all topics, commonly choosing questions
on the Paris Peace Conference, the League of Nations, the Collapse of International Order in the 1930s, and Namibian
History under German colonial rule.  As a result, most learners performed well on questions 1, 2, 3, and 5.

Markers    noted    significant    improvement    in    how    learners    answered    questions    B    and    C    compared    to    previous
years.  However, some learners still struggled to connect their content directly to the questions, especially in B
and C, indicating a need for more focused teaching on linking knowledge to question demands.
A common issue in question 2(a) was that learners discussed the League of Nations’ weaknesses without linking them
to the impact of the Paris Peace Conference, missing how initial conditions affected the League’s effectiveness.

Learners also showed limited knowledge of Namibian History under South African rule, as seen in question 6(a).  Many
confused facts from German colonial rule with those from the South African period.  This suggests that Namibian History
under South African rule was not fully studied or understood.

Recommendations for Teachers and Tutors
•	                                    Maintain   comprehensive   coverage   of   the   entire   syllabus   to   ensure   balanced   learner   development   and   continued
     improvement in overall performance.
•	                                    Emphasise the importance of explicitly linking historical content to the specific requirements of each exam question,
     guiding learners to address the question’s demands directly and effectively.
•	                                    Incorporate a diverse range of teaching resources including the Grade 9 syllabus and supplementary materials to
     deepen    learners’    understanding    of    Namibian    History    under    South  African    rule    and    to    prevent    confusion    with    the
     German colonial period.
•	                                    Adopt a thorough and systematic approach to teaching all sections of the syllabus, and support learners in making
     clear, logical connections between historical topics and examination questions.  This will further enhance learners’
     ability to construct well-informed, relevant responses.

GENERAL COMMENTS
The question paper was fair overall.  Most learners performed well on questions 1 and 5, but struggled with comparison
questions.  Learners should avoid answering sources in isolation; instead, they must compare similarities and differences
using their own words and provide inferences supported by evidence from both sources.  Synonyms should be used
rather than copying words directly from the sources.

Unlike the Ordinary level, learners must include contextual knowledge to explain similarities, differences, and to evaluate
the source.  Many learners lack contextual knowledge, which prevents them from interpreting sources effectively and
scoring higher marks.
For evaluation questions, learners must make clear choices and every inference or assertion must be supported by
evidence from the sources.  Testing the reliability of sources requires attention to four key elements:
1.  State if the source is reliable or not, with a reason.
2.  Consider the author ’s intention in publishing the source.
3.  Explain the significance of the date, using contextual knowledge.
4.  Identify the intended audience and the reaction expected.
For pictorial sources (cartoons, pictures, photographs), learners must make a choice, give an explanation, and support
it with evidence from the image, such as captions or visible details.  For the last two bonus marks, learners must test
the reliability of any two sources.
Teachers and tutors should focus on developing these skills and encourage learners to consult examiners’ reports for
further guidance.

To improve results in 2026:

1     Ensure learners develop the necessary skills for this exam to prevent poor performance.

2     Strengthen learners’ contextual knowledge for Depth Studies; limited knowledge leads to lower marks.

3     Help    learners    connect    recent    events    with    historical    ones    to    deepen    understanding    (e.g.,    link    the    fall    of
      communism to the USSR power struggle).

4     Emphasise content mastery, as a lack of knowledge hinders interpretation and explanation.

5     Train learners to compare sources accurately without copying or paraphrasing; use clear, direct
      comparisons (e.g., “In Source A, X... while in Source B, Y...”).

6     Continue improving the identification of differences between sources.

7     Teach learners to provide support that aligns with valid inferences, using evidence from both sources.

8     Practice writing purposes by focusing on explaining the author ’s intentions and intended audience response.

9     Regularly practice evaluating the usefulness and limitations of sources in class.

10    Prepare thoroughly for evaluation questions, such as those on “surprise” and “not surprise.”

11    Clarify that “not supporting” means the sources differ, while “supporting” means the sources agree.

12    Teach how to compare sources to identify agreements and disagreements.

13    For the final question, make a choice, quote directly from the sources, and explain using contextual knowledge.

14    Practice  evaluation  (testing  of  reliability)  on  any  two  sources  for  bonus  marks,  ensuring  it  aligns  with  the
      final question.

15    Do not use cross-referencing or contextual knowledge for bonus marks.

16    Avoid sharing marking schemes with learners, as they lack the necessary skills to interpret them.

17    Focus on teaching examination skills required for each question type, not on mark levels.

The paper was of similar standard as that of last year. The marks ranged from 0 to 75.

Although there was a general improvement in terms of the quality of work, it was observed that some candidates still
struggle with basic competences that should form part of their assumed knowledge.  For example, a candidate at this
level is expected to know the basic properties and formulae for geometric shapes such as a circle and a rhombus. A
candidate who struggles with such basic concepts, always finds the AS examination challenging.

Candidates are encouraged to show working always in order to gain method marks, even if their final answers may be
wrong.

Areas that still need improvement:

It is strongly recommended that the areas of improvement suggested in this report should be discussed with the
candidates thoroughly to avoid the candidates making the same mistakes year after year. It was quite worrisome that
although these points were raised in the previous reports, the candidates still continue to lose valuable marks. The
teachers are therefore advised to read these suggestions and advise the candidates accordingly.

1.    Candidates are encouraged to cancel any abandoned work before attempting to answer the question again.  If two
      answers are left on the same question, then the first answer seen will be marked. It’s a common practice by some
      candidates, especially when they are not sure of the answer, to write two answers and leave the marker to choose.
      This practice should be discouraged.


2.    If a candidate decides to use the additional page for answering any question, they must clearly cross out the
      abandoned work and refer the marker to the additional page.  For example, a candidate can write “See page 20”.
      This will make the marker aware that the question has been rewritten on the additional page.  If the candidate does
      not cross out the work on the original page, the work on the additional page is treated as a second answer, and will
      not be marked.


3.    For questions that require candidates to prove or show a quoted answer, they should write all the possible steps
      that lead to the proof, and state the quoted answer at the end.  The examiners mark what the candidate has written
      down, not what is implied.

4.    Although there was a slight improvement this year, it was still noted with concern that a number of candidates are
      failing    to    copy    the    figures    correctly    from    the    question.        Learners    who    misread    numbers    do    not    score    maximum
      marks      even      if      their      method      is      correct.            Candidates      must      read      and      copy      the      figures      carefully      when      answering
      questions.

      in    the    instructions    for    candidates.        Others    prefer    to    write    with    a    pencil    first    before    overwriting    with    a    pen.        This
      practice should be discouraged.

General Comments:
The paper was of a similar standard as that of last year. The marks ranged between 0 and 75. Most candidates finished
the paper.
It was clearly noticed that the candidates who entered this syllabus without a solid algebra foundation, were challenged
with the majority of the topics. Many candidates struggled with basic Ordinary Level competencies, like the factorisation
of trinomials and basic logarithmic laws.
It should be noted that the emphasis in AS is more on the method    and    the    mathematical    process    than    on    the    final
solution. Complete methods should be shown at all times.
Candidates must make sure to delete work that they do not want to be marked at the specific question.  It was seen that
some candidates approached a problem in two or three different ways, without deleting any of the work.  It was also
seen  that  questions  were  replaced  on  the  additional  page,  without  deleting  the  work  at  the  original  question.    In  these
cases, the work at the original question was marked.
If candidates want to use the additional page, they should clearly refer to the additional page at the appropriate question.
Candidates should be discouraged to work in pencil first and then to rewrite their work in pen.  They often do not copy
the pencil properly and some accuracy is lost after the pencil is erased.  In addition, it is more work and can result into
candidates not finishing the paper.
Centres must NOT                                                                                                                                                                                       provide any additional paper.  Candidates do their work on these papers and then just copy the
answers, which results in the loss of all the marks for the specific question.
It is advisable that answers should be left exact where possible.  An answer of                                                           is exact and is preferred above the
decimal version of 5.38516… .
Many candidates were very careless with the rounding instructions throughout this paper.  It is always advisable to write
the complete values throughout the working, before attempting to round the final answer.  This prevents the loss of
accuracy caused by premature rounding.
It was clear that some candidates confused significant figures and decimal places.
Most candidates took care to show their working, which allows them to gain marks for correct methods even when their
answers are wrong.  However, candidates should be encouraged to show complete methods, especially when they are
asked to prove a quoted answer.  Candidates may NOT work backwards from the quoted answer.
Candidates should realise that questions are structured in an attempt to help them.  The earlier parts of a question are
often used in subsequent parts.  The word “HENCE” is an indication that the previous answer                                                                                                                                     must be used in order to
solve the specific question.  Candidates must be taught how to interpret questions of this nature.  If the question states
“hence” and the previous question is not used, no marks may be awarded for the solution.
More care should be taken in the classroom with the mathematical notation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           and the teaching of the relevant terminology.
Teachers  and  learners  should  not  only  concentrate  on  the  final  answer,  but  also  on  the  accuracy  of  the  mathematical
writing.  For example, it was often extremely difficult to decide whether a candidate meant sin2x or sin 2x.

calculator settings from degrees into radians.  Candidates should be taught that they must immediately change their
calculators to the correct setting once they read a question.

Candidates must                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  not use tables to draw basic exponential,

Key messages

•	   Learners	are	sometimes	unable	to	gain	full	credit	because	their	descriptions	are	not	given	with	sufficient	detail,	and
     they	would	benefit	from	providing	more	detail.		Often	answers	are	made	unclear	through	the	omission	of	certain	key
     words	and	inappropriate	use	of	everyday	language.
•	   Learners	should	avoid	prematurely	rounding	interim	answers	within	a	calculation	as	this	can	lead	to	the	final	answer
     given	on	the	answer	line	being	incorrect.

•	   Please	note:		Numerical	answers	may	not	be	given	as	fractions,	in	terms	of	pi	or	in	surd	form.		Although	this	is	more
     accurate,	candidates	must	show	correct	rounding.
•	   Learners	should	use	the	number	of	significant	figures	in	the	question	data	as	a	guide	to	the	number	of	significant
     figures	required	in	the	final	answer.	In	the	vast	majority	of	cases	a	minimum	of	two	significant	figures	is	appropriate
     for	the	final	answer.	 	Please	refer	to	the	syllabus,	page	5,	bullet	5	of	Arithmetics:	 	“take	account	of	accuracy	in
     numerical	work	and	handle	calculations	so	that	significant	figures	are	neither	lost	unnecessarily	nor	carried	beyond
     what	is	justified.”

•	   Learners	should	pay	particular	attention	to	the	prefixes	of	units.		It	these	are	ignored	or	interpreted	incorrectly,	it	can
     lead	to	a	power-of-ten	error	in	the	final	answer.
•	   In	numerical	calculations,	learners	should	remember	to	first	write	down	the	appropriate	symbol	equation,	using	the
     CORRECT	symbols,	before	substituting	in	the	relevant	values.	If	the	equation	is	rearranged,	the	new	subject	of
     the	equation	should	always	be	stated.		Learners	should	avoid	to	show	their	working	with	an	expression	that	does
     not	have	a	subject.	 	There	are	times	when	the	subject	changes	because	of	changes	made.	 	Rearrangement	of
     equations	is	only	possible	with	the	inclusion	of	the	subject.
•	   Many	questions	at	AS	Level	require	learners	to	perform	unit	conversions,	for	example	from	mm2	to	m2	or	from	g
     to	kg.		Errors	due	to	incorrect	unit	conversions	can	add	up	over	a	number	of	different	question	parts	and	make	a
     significant	difference	to	the	final	mark	for	the	paper.		Learners	should	continually	practise	converting	between	units
     when	performing	calculations.
•	   Learners	should	read	each	question	carefully	before	answering.	It	is	important	to	avoid	merely	scanning	the	question
     as	important	instructions	may	be	overlooked.

•	   For	AS-level	physics,	learners	need	to	be	comfortable	using	physics	formulae	where	more	than	one	variable	is
     substituted.		Solving	equations	using	variables	is	essential	mathematics	here.
•	   It	is	important	that	learners	practise	answering	questions	that	are	of	the	same	standard	as	those	in	the	examination.
     Working	through	past	papers	is	a	way	of	achieving	this.

•	   Some	credit	is	awarded	for	the	application	and	extension	of	the	content	of	the	syllabus.		In	order	to	score	highly,
     learners	need	to	have	a	thorough	understanding	of	the	subject	matter	so	that	they	can	discuss	sensibly	situations
     that	are	based	on	the	theoretical	work.

GENERAL COMMENTS
The NSSCAS 8225 Physics Paper 3 for 2025 was the fifth cohort since the first implementation of the subject NSSCAS
8225 Physics in 2021.  The overall standard of the paper was similar to that of the first four cohorts of (2021 to 2024).
The candidates’ performance, on average, appeared similar to the previous cohorts.

What  was  significant  in  the  2024  series  is  that  the  quality  of  the  Supervisors’  results  was  often  centre  dependent.   At
some    centres,    the    Supervisor ’s    Reports    received    included    sets    of    numerical    results    for    the    experiments,    as    well    as
additional     useful     details     about     difficulties     encountered     in     the     experiments,     plus     any     help     given     to     candidates.         This
was   impressive   and   supervisors   at   these   centres   are   commended   for   the   job   well   done.      For   instance,   in   regards   to
question    2,    strong    centres    reported    challenges    with    the    petri    dishes.       The    subject    teachers’    confidential    instructions
specify that the two petri dishes to be provided to candidates should be both made from plastic and should both have an
approximate height of 14 mm.  There was only expected to be a difference in diameter, and the recommended diameter
specified in the confidential instructions is 65 mm and 80 mm for the smaller and larger petri dishes respectively.  In the
supervisors,   reports   from   these   strong   centres,   evidence   was   provided   about   any   deviations   for   instance   in   the   type
of   material,   diameter   and   height   of   petri   dishes.      For   question   1,   evidence   was   also   provided   about   the   deviations   in
the height of the retort stands, the use of slotted masses instead of the specified pendulum bob / mass piece, and the
deviation in the mass of the pendulum bob / mass piece.  This evidence was taken into account in the marking process.
The candidates could be awarded credit if the values obtained were outside the range specified in the question paper,
but within the range of the Supervisor ’s data.
Just like the quality of the Supervisors’ results, the general standard and performance of the work done by the candidates
was  also  more  often  than  not,  centre  dependent.    On  the  one  hand,  there  were  many  excellent  scripts  by  candidates
who    had    been    well    prepared    for    the    practical    paper,    and    they    demonstrated    their    skills    in    measuring,    recording    and
processing their results.  On the other hand, in some centres, the candidates appeared unprepared.  This was evident
especially   in   Question   2 (g).      Candidates   who   were   not   well   prepared   often   referred   to   uncertainties,   limitations   and
improvements associated with question 1 rather than focusing only on question 2.

KEY MESSAGES
•     Candidates need to remember to state their recorded measurements to the appropriate degree of precision which
      is    consistent    the    measuring    instruments    used.    For    instance,    in   1 (a), 1 (c),                                                                              D    and                             H    should    be    recorded    to    the
      nearest mm, e.g. 70.0 cm, 31.5 cm.  Similarly, in 2 (a) (i) and                                                                                      2 (d),                                            d and                   h should be recorded to the nearest mm,
      e.g. 6.5 cm, 8.0 cm, 1.4 cm.  These are all consistent with the precision of the ruler / metre rule used to take these
      measurements. In 1 (b), 1 (c), the time T should be recorded to the nearest 0.1 s or 0.01 s.
•     If a raw value is out of trend to that expected, candidates should be encouraged to check the readings again with
      the equipment provided in the early stages of data collection.
•     In the table work, the number of significant figures in the calculated quantity should relate to the number of significant
      figures   in   the   raw   data   with   the   least   number   of   significant   figures.      Each   calculated   quantity   should   be   checked
      row by row.  It is unnecessary, and often incorrect, to force the number of significant figures to be constant down a
      column of calculated values.  The number of significant figures may, if necessary, vary down a column of values for
      a calculated quantity.
•     In     the     graphical     work,     candidates     should     be     able     to     read     off     any     points     to     the     nearest     half     a     small     square.          In
      particular,     candidates     should     check     carefully     the     read-offs     of     points     used     in     the     gradient     calculation     and     when
      determining the y-intercept.
•     When    justifying    a    number    of    significant    figures    in    a    calculated    quantity,    candidates    should    relate    the    number    of
      significant figures in the quantity to the raw readings used in the calculation.  Candidates should not use the phrase
      ‘raw  readings’  without  explaining  what  those  readings  are,  or  attempt  to  use  intermediate  calculated  quantities  to
      justify the number of significant figures.
•     To        be        successful        answering     Question 2,        candidates        should        be        reminded        that        their        identified        limitations        and
      suggestions for improvement must be focused on the particular experiment being carried out.  General points such
      as   ‘measurements   were   difficult’   or   ‘use   more   precise   measuring   instruments’   will   not   usually   gain   credit   without
      further detail.

2      (e) (ii)      Successful candidates had three steps in their argument.  They first stated a criterion to be used
                     for testing the relationship.  This could be a percentage uncertainty that they think is a sensible
                     limit   for                                           this   particular   experiment,   e.g.   5%,   10%   or   20%.      Next   they   calculate   the   percentage
                     difference  between  their  values  of  k.    Finally,  they  compare  the  percentage  difference  between
                     their       k       values       to       the       percentage       uncertainty       chosen       and       decide       whether       the       relationship       is
                     supported or not supported.  If the percentage difference between the two k values is less than
                     the stated criterion, these successful answers then say that the relationship is supported.  If the
                     value of the percentage difference is greater than the value of the percentage uncertainty stated
                     as the criterion, then the relationship is not supported.  The candidates should make an explicit
                     statement,   e.g.   ‘the   relationship   is   not   supported’.      Some   candidates   did   not   give   any   criterion
                     to   test   against.      Many   statements   were   too   vague.      Some   candidates   looked   at   the   difference
                     without determining a percentage, or gave an answer that did not logically follow from the data.
                     These could not be awarded credit.

              going   through   the   experiment   systematically   and   stating   clearly   each   difficulty.      Candidates   should
